title: Cato
description: Addison's serious tragedy of the last days of Cato of Utica, written as a demonstration that regular neoclassical drama in blank verse could teach Stoic virtue and resignation to providence. It was the most acted, read and imitated English tragedy of the first half of the eighteenth century.
plot_or_argument: After Thapsus the defeated Cato refuses Caesar's clemency and holds Utica; his friend Lucilius dies by poison in a scene of Stoic obedience, the treachery of Sempronius is exposed, and Juba's suit for Marcia fails; Cato secures the safety of those about him, reconciles public liberty with resignation to providence, and kills himself, the catastrophe being reported rather than shown.
narrative_structure: Five-act regular tragedy closely observing the unities of time, place and action, moving from the council at Utica through the discovery of the conspiracy to the protagonist's suicide and its reportage.
principal_characters: Cato; Caesar; Lucilius; Sempronius; Marcia; Juba
literary_form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat blank verse of the moderated post-Dryden line, with balanced antithetical periods and sententious closures; the speeches are built as declamatory rhetorical units.
historical_context: First performed at Drury Lane in the spring of 1713, during the party struggle over the peace settlement, when the theatre was an arena of political interpretation; the play was praised in The Tatler in the season of its first performance, and the rival Whig and Tory press each claimed it.
literary_significance: It fixed for a generation the model of the rational moral tragedy and made Roman liberty and Christian resignation a national schoolroom exemplum, admired across party lines, imitated on the stage and in the closet, and answered by the later tragedy of feeling.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; Addison's authorship is documented by his own publication and by contemporary correspondence.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in octavo in 1713 and reissued frequently with variant title-page wording; standard modern reading text is in the scholarly editions of Addison's plays. The exact first-day performance date is not asserted here.

title: The Spectator and Tatler Papers (Addison)
description: Addison's contribution to the daily and weekly essay papers he conducted with Steele: the club and character papers, the imagination essays, the Milton criticism, the pastoral series and the oriental tales, which together made the polite essay the century's instrument of everyday moral judgment.
plot_or_argument: Mr. Spectator, who has resolved neither to laugh nor to be serious, presents himself and the club of which he is the silent censor, then reports the speeches, projects and follies of its members and of the citizens, families and readers whose letters arrive at his desk.
narrative_structure: A serial miscellany of short unsigned-to-signed papers, framed by a recurring persona and an intermittently advancing club narrative, with inset tales, letters to the editor and critical dissertations.
principal_characters: Mr. Spectator; Sir Roger de Coverley; Sir Andrew Freeport; Will Honeycomb; Captain Sentry; the club of the Spectator; the letter-writing public
meter_and_prosody: Prose in the balanced middle style Addison theorised, with periodic sentences, tagged couplet quotations from the poets, and the rhythmically clause-balanced close; the papers on verse discuss the couplet and blank verse explicitly.
historical_context: The daily Spectator ran from March 1711 to December 1712 and was revived weekly in 1714, exploiting coffee-house and tea-table reading, the provincial postal network and the lapse of the licensing Act; the Addison-Steele partnership divided the papers unevenly and ended in public coolness.
literary_significance: Addison's papers gave English prose its most widely taught model, invented the character-based periodical essay, and with the imagination and Milton essays installed a criticism of taste and genius inside neoclassical rules.
attribution_notes: Collaborative by formation: the papers were produced by Addison and Steele together, with contributions from Hughes, Berkeley, Miss Manley and others; individual ascriptions in the early numbers remain partly conjectural, and this record covers the Addisonian share.
bibliographical_notes: Issued daily and weekly in folio numbers and collected in octavo volumes from 1711 onwards, with variant issue numbering; the standard scholarly division of the papers is by the edition of the daily Spectator's numbering.

title: The Freeholder
alternative_titles: The Freeholder: a Collection of Papers
description: Addison's late political essay paper, written in support of the Hanoverian settlement during the Jacobite rising of 1715 and addressed to the freeholder electorate; it argues the case for limited property-based liberty against both arbitrary power and popular licence.
plot_or_argument: A freeholder addresses his constituents and a succession of imaginary opponents, tracing the constitution from the feudal conquest, defending the settled succession, and warning that a standing army, Jacobite intrigue and the demagogic temper threaten the same liberty from opposite sides.
narrative_structure: A short serial of letter-like papers addressed to a named friend or to the freeholders, each taking up one branch of the argument, with an inserted historical dissertation.
principal_characters: the freeholder-writer; the party opponent; the Jacobite conspirator
meter_and_prosody: Clear argumentative prose of the Spectator manner, with heavy use of balanced pairs, historical example and closing sententiae.
historical_context: Published during and immediately after the '15 rising, in the season of Whig pamphlet warfare that also produced Swift's and Steele's party papers and Addison's breach with Steele over The Drummer's circle.
literary_significance: It became a standard textbook of the moderate Whig constitutional argument, reprinted in America through the 1760s and 1770s as an elementary school of British liberty.
attribution_notes: Addison's authorship is uncontested, though the paper was issued without his name; his official connection with the administration has encouraged readers to treat it as ministerial writing.
bibliographical_notes: The papers appeared in 1715-16 and were collected in a single volume; enlarged and revised issues followed in Addison's lifetime, and the last to bear his hand is dated 1719.

title: Remarks on Several Parts of Paradise Lost
description: Addison's serial criticism of Milton's epic, first conducted as papers in The Spectator: it reads Paradise Lost as a work of sublime original genius disciplined by scriptural and classical learning, and defends its machinery, its diction and its allegory against the objections of the French neoclassical rules.
plot_or_argument: Successive remarks take the fable, the characters, the machinery of angels, the episodes of limbo and of Pandemonium, the similes and the versification, arguing that Milton's faults are those of a genius and that his subject gives him a sublimity the classical epics could not reach.
narrative_structure: A linked sequence of short critical dissertations, one per paper, each opening on a passage and closing with a general rule of taste.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of exemplary periodic balance, continuously reinforced by quoted hexameter and couplet passages from Milton and the ancients.
historical_context: Delivered in the year of the quarrel over the unities and over the value of blank verse, when Tonson's cheap Milton and Dennis's and Bentley's rival criticisms made the national epic a contested property.
literary_significance: It established the Augustan rehabilitation of Milton and, through its account of the sublime and of allegorical machinery, supplied the vocabulary that later eighteenth-century criticism and the graveyard poets inherited.
attribution_notes: Uncontested Addison; a single passage's share has occasionally been queried by bibliographers of the joint paper.
bibliographical_notes: First printed among the daily Spectator papers of 1712; separately revised and prefixed to later Milton editions, the enlarged issue commonly dated 1719.

title: The Italian Opera
description: Addison's satiric essay on the Italian opera then occupying the London stage, a comic indictment of declamatory singing, castrato heroes, improbable machinery and the abdication of sense before sound.
plot_or_argument: The spectator reports the absurdities of an evening at the Italian opera, where artificial voices command armies and melt away in affected rapture, stage machinery manufactures thunder, and the audience most admires whatever most forbids belief.
narrative_structure: A single character paper: expository frame, catalogued instances of abuse, and a closing general reflection on credulity and taste.
principal_characters: Mr. Spectator; the opera singers; the applauding audience
meter_and_prosody: Lucid ironic prose, with exaggerated enumeration and the mock-solemn aside; the paper's couplet tag is quoted from the poets of the theatre.
historical_context: Written while Handel and Handel's rivals were establishing Italian heroica opera at the Queen's Theatre, and while the English opera, the ballad entertainment and the spoken drama were competing for the same audience; the paper belongs to the long quarrel between English spoken theatre and foreign sung drama.
literary_significance: It set the terms of the English critique of operatic convention for the century, and was reused by Gay and by the ballad-opera writers of 1728 as the obvious target of their burlesque.
attribution_notes: Standardly assigned to Addison, but the earliest Spectator numbers divide between Addison and Steele and the ascription rests on style and on the later collected arrangement rather than on external documentation.
bibliographical_notes: First printed among the daily Spectator papers of 1711 and reprinted in the collected volumes; the specific serial number is not asserted in this record.

title: The Tatler Papers
description: Richard Steele's three-times-weekly paper, conducted under the mask of Isaac Bickerstaff Esq., which turned the newsbook, the coffee-room gossip and the character sketch into a morally reformed periodical and created the English essay paper.
plot_or_argument: Mr. Speculator and his correspondents report the clubs, the play-house, the opera, the town and the country, alternating manners, marriage and duelling stories with party politics and with praise of Addison's Cato and of private virtue.
narrative_structure: Serial papers distributed among fixed stations of observation (the coffee-house, the theatre, Kit-Cat, the opera, the country), with a lightly advancing fictional biography of the editor and of his correspondents.
principal_characters: Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.; the Speculator; cousin Jenny; Will Honeycomb; the Whig and Tory clubs; the readers who write to the editor
meter_and_prosody: A looser, more colloquial and syntactically broken style than Addison's, full of ellipsis, exclamation and half-unfinished sentences, which Steele's imitators took for the natural tone of feeling.
historical_context: Launched in April 1709 and running to the beginning of 1711, the Tatler exploited the new cheap journalism after the lapse of licensing, the party pressure of the Sacheverell trial years, and Steele's continuing interest in the reformation of the stage.
literary_significance: It made periodical moral commentary a profession and a literary form, and its account of the affective, tearful reform of manners prepared sentimental comedy and the novel of character.
attribution_notes: Principally Steele's, with a substantial early contribution from Addison and papers from Hughes, Berkeley, Prior and others; the joint numbers are still disputed by bibliographers.
bibliographical_notes: Published in folio numbers from April 1709, collected in volume form from 1710, and revised by Steele for the collected editions; the volumes carry the Bickerstaff mask and the later Merlin's Cave intelligence. The full title-page wording varies between issues and is not asserted here.

title: The Conscious Lovers
description: Steele's five-act comedy of sensibility, modelled on Terence and rewritten to substitute tender feeling and generous self-command for the wit and rake of the Restoration stage; the most influential example of the laughing-and-crying reform of English comedy.
plot_or_argument: Young Bevil, torn between duty to his father's choice and love for Indiana, discovers that the girl he has rescued from slavery in Turkey is the daughter of his father's presumed dead friend, so that his benevolence is rewarded by a match both honourable and affectionate; the subplot of Myrtle and the betraying Humphrey secures the second pair.
narrative_structure: Regular five-act comedy with a double plot, anagnorisis deferred to the final discovery and a prologue and epilogue framing the moral argument about the theatre.
principal_characters: Young Bevil; Indiana; Sir John Bevil; Myrtle; Leonora; Isabella; Humphrey; Cimber
meter_and_prosody: Prose dialogue of polished conversational ease, interrupted by set speeches of feeling whose periodic rhythm imitates oratory rather than wit.
historical_context: Performed at Drury Lane in the season after Steele's return from Ireland and his quarrel with Addison, and acted in the same years as the dispute over laughter in comedy which culminated in Fielding's defence of humour.
literary_significance: It made the hero of sensibility respectable on the London stage, supplied the pattern of the reformed sentimental comedy for three decades, and gave the century its clearest statement that virtue rewarded by feeling is the proper business of the drama.
attribution_notes: Uncontested Steele, though his borrowings from the Andria of Terence and from previous French plots are extensive and were noticed by the reviewers.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in quarto in 1722 with the dedicatory and critical preface on the stage; the prologue and epilogue were delivered at the first performance, whose exact date is not asserted here.

title: The Guardian Papers
description: Steele's thrice-weekly paper of 1713, conducted in the guardian mask and chiefly against the deism of Anthony Collins, the free-thinkers, the pretenders and the married men's project; the most openly party-political of the essay papers and the occasion of the Addison-Steele breach.
plot_or_argument: The guardian reports the transactions of his ward, the public, attacks the trick of ridicule against religion, stages the Married Men's claim to be governed by their wives, and defends the Christian foundation of moral obligation.
narrative_structure: Serial papers alternating party argument, fictional letter and project, character writing and the dialogue between the guardian and his correspondents.
principal_characters: Mr. Guardian; the Married Men; the female correspondents; the free-thinker
meter_and_prosody: Colloquial, urgent argumentative prose with the interrupted sentence and the indignant apostrophe, less periodic than Addison's.
historical_context: Published in the months of the Asylum Bill and the fall of the Harley ministry, when Steele turned from the moderate essay to high-church and Whig polemic; the paper's attack on the Married Men drew the rebuttals of the female writers of the period.
literary_significance: It documents the moment at which the periodical essay became an instrument of party and of religious polemic, and its controversy with the anti-theatrical and deist press shaped the later eighteenth-century debate on ridicule and morality.
attribution_notes: Chiefly Steele's, with numbers by Addison, Hughes, Prior and Berkeley; the disputed shares are the occasion of one of the century's first collaborations dissolving in print.
bibliographical_notes: Numbers ran from March 1713; the papers were collected in volume form the same year, and the edition varies between the issue and the collected text.

title: The Christian Hero
alternative_titles: The Christian Hero: An Argument, That no Principles can be effectual to encourage Vertue and Goodness, but those of Christianity
description: Steele's devotional and moral argument that unassisted virtue is unsustainable and that Christianity supplies the only adequate motive to goodness; a confession of his own past profligacy and the book he feared would be thrown in his teeth.
plot_or_argument: The author proves from experience and from the passions that honour, interest and good nature leave a man unprotected against himself, then argues that the Christian rule alone both forbids and enables, and closes with the picture of the hero of piety.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in numbered sections, moving from autobiography and diagnosis through scriptural proof to the exemplary character.
principal_characters: the penitent author; the man of the world
meter_and_prosody: Plain, earnest, familiar prose, deliberately free of ornament, with the short imperative sentence and direct address to the reader.
historical_context: Written early in Steele's army years and published as his public career made him a target, at the height of the deist and anti-deist controversy and in the year of his quarrel with Addison and of his entry into party politics.
literary_significance: It is the periodical essay's other face, the serious religious self-examination that made Steele's name a byword for professional conscience, and it supplied the model of the reforming tract of the century.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Composition date follows Steele's own account of the tract's origin in his military years; it ran through several editions in its first year and was reissued under slightly varied title wording.

title: The Drummer
alternative_titles: The Drummer; Or, the Haunted House
description: The comedy of the haunted house and the alarming drum, printed in 1716 in a text that represents Steele's earlier The Funeral of 1701 heavily revised; it is the published trace of the Addison-Steele partnership working on one play after the rupture of the essay papers.
plot_or_argument: The ghostly apparatus of a haunted house is engineered by a scheming butler and a counterfeit spirit to secure the heroine; a cowardly fife and drum scare, a rival suitor, and the exposure of the trick resolve into the marriage of the man who has shown real courage.
narrative_structure: Regular five-act comedy of intrigue and humours, with the burlesque ghost-plot as the mechanism of discovery.
principal_characters: the heiress and her mother; the two rival suitors; the servants who stage the ghostly fraud; the drummer whose signal frightens the house
meter_and_prosody: Prose dialogue with the song interpolations characteristic of the early eighteenth-century afterpiece comedy.
historical_context: Acted and printed at Drury Lane in 1716, in the settled years after the failure of the Jacobite rising, when the ghost comedy and the operatic machine were competing with reformed moral comedy for the same audience.
literary_significance: It documents the dissolution of the Addison-Steele collaboration in the same medium that had made it famous, and it is the period's clearest instance of a play remade by one partner's hand under another's name.
attribution_notes: Collaborative and displaced: the ground plot belongs to Steele's The Funeral of 1701, the printed 1716 text was revised and enlarged with new scenes and songs generally assigned to Addison, and prefatory matter has been variously distributed between the two writers; the record is placed with Steele because the design and the earlier version are his.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1716 under the title The Drummer, with the preface; earlier and later states of the text differ in the distribution of scenes between the two hands.

title: Pastorals
description: Pope's four seasonal pastorals, printed when he was barely twenty and presented by him as the exercise of his earliest years: a Virgilian and Spenserian apprenticeship poem which nevertheless displays the couplet manner, the panegyric structure and the critical self-fashioning of his mature work.
plot_or_argument: Shepherd speakers answer one another through spring, summer, autumn and winter, each season drawing its own song, lament or tribute; the sequence carries Pope's early commendation of Addison and of the military glory of the recent war inside the conventional eclogue.
narrative_structure: Four separately titled eclogues in dialogue, arranged as a year and each closing with a song or a panegyric passage.
principal_characters: the shepherd speakers of the four seasons; the presiding Muse
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed heroic couplets, lengthened and made melodious by Spenserian and Miltonic example, with shorter lyric stanzas for the embedded songs.
historical_context: Printed in the sixth part of Tonson's Poetical Miscellanies in 1709, in the same years as Ambrose Philips's own pastorals; the ensuing dispute about priority, about the proper diction of shepherds and about the value of Spenser made the pastorals the opening battle of the century's quarrel over rules and genius.
literary_significance: It announced the couplet style and the doctrine of imitation on which Pope's whole career depended, and it supplied the Dunciad with one of its longest-lived personal grievances.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though Pope's claim to have written the poems as a boy is supported partly by his own later testimony rather than by independent evidence.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Tonson's Poetical Miscellanies, 2 May 1709; revised and re-collected in Pope's Works of 1717, where the prefatory account restates the claim of early composition.

title: An Essay on Criticism
description: Pope's verse treatise on the rules of taste: it argues that criticism is a polite and necessary art learned from nature and from the ancients, catalogs the vices of partial, arrogant and pedantic judging, and ends by demanding that the critic's manners answer the critic's learning.
plot_or_argument: The first movement derives the laws of judging from the practice of nature and of the classical writers; the second catalogs the causes of false taste, pride, partiality and the worship of parts; the third passes from the ancients to the moderns, to the French rules, and to the moral duty of candid, instructive criticism.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in numbered parts, each built as a succession of linked sententiae and examples rather than as narrative.
principal_characters: the poet-critic; the false critic; the ancients as a court of appeal
meter_and_prosody: Closed heroic couplets of exceptional regularity, with the balanced antithetical line, run-on enjambed passages for difficulty, and deliberate sound-imitation of the sense being described.
historical_context: Published in the year between Windsor-Forest and the Rape of the Lock, when Rymer's and Dennis's dramatic controversy, Temple's ancient-modern essay and Addison's periodical criticism had made the rules of art a popular subject; the essay consolidates the Shaftesburian and neoclassical language of taste.
literary_significance: It became the century's handbook of critical common sense, supplied the durable phrases by which English criticism discussed wit, nature and the rules, and fixed the couplet as the vehicle of serious argument.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1711 and corrected through the editions of Pope's lifetime; the passage later numbered as a fourth part was added in a revised issue of the following decade, and the priority of the several states is not asserted here.

title: Windsor-Forest
description: Pope's topographical poem from the view over Windsor and the Thames, which reads a surveyed landscape as the evidence of a harmonious order in nature, in the British past and in the commercial present, and closes in a prophecy of national peace and plenty.
plot_or_argument: The poet surveys the prospect from the forest, descends to the Thames and its fishing and trading, reviews the violent history of Britain from the conquest and the civil wars, and resolves the spectacle into a providential harmony of the elements and of the realm.
narrative_structure: A single topographical sweep from prospect to river to history to prophecy, held together by the couplet's reflective transitions rather than by action.
principal_characters: the poet; the Thames; the genius of the place; the bird and beast inhabitants of the forest
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of ceremonious regularity, with the long descriptive passage, the apostrophe and the closing epilogic couplet.
historical_context: Published in the closing months of the negotiation of the peace that ended the War of the Spanish Succession, and addressed in its first state to the peace and to the royal seat; the poem's Whig language of liberty, trade and improved property belongs to the estate-poetry vogue of these years.
literary_significance: It renewed Denham's Cooper's Hill for the eighteenth century and made the surveyed landscape the occasion for a national argument about order, commerce and providence; its river and forest writing is the direct precedent of Thomson.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First issued separately in 1713 and revised in the Works of 1717, where the closing panegyric is re-addressed to the changed succession; the several states of that conclusion differ in wording.

title: The Rape of the Lock
alternative_titles: The Rape of the Lock: A Heroic Poem
description: Pope's mock-heroic poem on the theft of a lock of a young woman's hair, which deploys epic machinery, invocations and catalogue in the service of a card-table, a dressing-room and a scissors, and turns a family quarrel into an analysis of the economy of female beauty and reputation.
plot_or_argument: Belinda sleeps while Ariel, her guardian sylph, warns her of an impending mischance; at Hampton the Baron, aided by a love-lorn gnome, cuts the lock amid a catalogue of her treasures; the resulting breach of the two families is fought as a battle of wits and tongues, and the lock itself is lost in the air and enshrined among the constellations.
narrative_structure: An enlarged epic argument in cantos, with invocation, machinery, catalogue, descent to the underworld of melancholy and a metamorphic conclusion; the first version is shorter and lacks the Rosicrucian machinery.
principal_characters: Belinda; the Baron; Ariel; Umbriel; Thalestris; the sylphs and gnomes; the man of art
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets, with the sustained mock-epic simile, the invocation and the epic enumeration adjusted to the scale of a trinket.
historical_context: Written to laugh down the quarrel between two Roman Catholic families over the cutting of a lock, and published in the years when the tea-table, the assembly and the luxury pamphlets were making female fashion a subject of moral argument; the poem's burlesque of machinery also answers the vogue for the rosea-crossa occult philosophy.
literary_significance: It created the mock-epic as a fully serious form in English and remains the period's most exact analysis of a society in which value attaches to appearance; it set the pattern imitated by the century's other lowering of the sublime.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1712 in three cantos; the enlarged edition of five cantos with the added machinery appeared in 1714 and was revised in later issues, with the passage of the cave of spleen and the concluding catastrophe variously handled.

title: Verses to the Memory of an Unfortunate Lady
alternative_titles: An Epistle to an Unfortunate Lady
description: Pope's blank-verse monologue of a banished woman dying abroad, who charges her friends not to mourn her and asks only that her urn be carried home; an early English example of the rhetoric of obscurity, exile and unremembered death.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, an outcast from her own country and betrayed by the man she loved, dictates from her deathbed the terms of her burial, refuses the pomp of mourning, and reflects on the fate of women whose passion has destroyed their reputation.
narrative_structure: A single continuous apostrophic address, moving from the charge to the friends, through the memory of the betrayal, to the prophecy of an unknown grave.
principal_characters: the unfortunate lady; the absent friend addressed; the unworthy lover
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the elevated Miltonic manner, with strong enjambment and Latinate inversion.
historical_context: Printed among the poems collected in 1717, in the years when the Catholic exile and the concealed nunnery were live political subjects and when the graveyard meditation was beginning to form as a mode.
literary_significance: It is the earliest English poem to make the un mourned dead woman a subject of sustained blank-verse reflection, and it prepares the path from the couplet public to the meditative lyric of the mid-century.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the collected poems of 1717, where it was prefaced with a short argument; the date of composition is not securely established and is left null here.

title: Eloisa to Abelard
description: Pope's verse epistle from Heloise to Abelard, written in the Ovidian manner as a confession of a love that the convent cannot extinguish; the poem analyses the passion of religious and erotic love confused in one mind.
plot_or_argument: Eloisa, abbess in the cloister, writes to the man who has abandoned her to her vows: she recounts her education and their love, argues with her own guilt, and resolves finally to preserve his fame by her silence and her unhappiness.
narrative_structure: A single letter in verse, progressing from address to narrative memory, to self-examination and passion's quarrel with duty, to a closing resolution.
principal_characters: Eloisa; Abelard
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets made nervous by exclamation, apostrophe and broken syntax, the periodic closure repeatedly delayed by the passion it describes.
historical_context: Written after the letters of Abelard and Heloise had been made English and adapted by the early-eighteenth-century theatre, and in the same season as the controversy over female desire and the convent in the Gothic and sentimental tale.
literary_significance: It gave English poetry its most quoted study of a woman's divided consciousness, and it became the standard model for the poetic epistle of feeling for half a century.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the collected poems of 1717; Pope reissued it with small revision in later editions of his separate poems.

title: Ode for Music
description: Pope's irregular ode written for musical setting, an attempt to carry the English Pindaric of Dryden into a theory of music's powers over the passions and over the elements.
plot_or_argument: The poem calls on music to descend and to rule the heart, traces its effects through the passions from terror to pity and love, and ends by claiming that the composer's art can remake the hearer's soul.
narrative_structure: A strophic irregular ode, each stanza taking one power of music, with an invocation opening and a panegyric close.
meter_and_prosody: A Pindaric stanza of long and short five-beat and four-beat lines with a varied rhyme scheme, written to be set; the verse imitates the progressions of the music it praises.
historical_context: Composed in the same year as Windsor-Forest, when English odes were being written for Handel's London season and for the theatre's incidental music, and when the powers of music were a standard subject of the periodical essay.
literary_significance: It is the most accomplished of the early eighteenth-century odes written for composition and a document of the period's attempt to refound the sublime on music rather than on versification.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1712 and reprinted in the collected poems of 1717; the commissioning occasion and any performance history are not established for this record, and the first_performance_date is left null.

title: The Iliad of Homer
alternative_titles: The Iliad of Homer Translated from the Greek
description: Pope's complete translation of the Iliad, issued in parts by subscription and then in volumes: the most commercially successful and most criticised English Homer, which recast Greek epic as Augustan heroic couplet and as a national monument.
plot_or_argument: The translation follows Homer's argument from the plague and the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon through the great battles, the embassy, the death of Patroclus and the vengeance on Hector, to the ransoming of the body, with the accompanying scholarly notes and the essay on the genius and writings of Homer.
narrative_structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the twenty-four books of the Iliad, published in installments and collected in volumes, each with argument, notes and classical apparatus.
principal_characters: Achilles; Hector; Agamemnon; Patroclus; Priam; Homer as the translated author
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet sustained over the longest English poem of the century, with the epic simile compressed into the closed pair and the line-end made the unit of judgment.
historical_context: Subscribed for at the height of the war's aftermath and of the classical vogue, it was attacked for its fidelity by Bentley and by the scholars, defended by the fashionable, and made the centre of the quarrel over the study of the ancients; its subscription model also made Pope the century's first profiting English poet.
literary_significance: For a century it was the English Homer, the book by which the epics were known to readers of verse; at once the monument of Augustan neoclassicism and the translation that later critics, from Blake to the Victorian Hellenists, chose to destroy.
attribution_notes: Pope's own hand, working with a library of Latin, French and English commentators and with the help of friends on the notes; the verse translation itself is not divided among several writers.
bibliographical_notes: The first volumes appeared in 1715 and the completed translation was collected in six volumes by 1720; the several issues differ in their plates, arguments and notes.

title: The Odyssey of Homer
description: Pope's translation of the Odyssey, published in volumes with the scholarly apparatus and the essay on Homer's genius, and completed largely by under-writers whose share Pope acknowledged in his advertisement.
plot_or_argument: The translation follows the wanderings of Ulysses from Calypso's island, through the Phaeacian court and the cyclops, Circe and the lower world, to the return to Ithaca and the destruction of the suitors.
narrative_structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the twenty-four books of the Odyssey, published in installments with arguments and notes.
principal_characters: Ulysses; Penelope; Telemachus; the suitors; the gods of the poem
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet, commonly judged looser, flatter and more mechanical than that of the Iliad, a difference often attributed to the share of the assisting hands.
historical_context: Issued after the Iliad and after the Homeric quarrels with the scholars, in the season when subscription was giving way to the booksellers' market; the volume was pirated and its assistant translators later figured among the tribe of the Dunciad.
literary_significance: It completed the Augustan Homer and became the standard example of the assisted, commercialised great translation, raising the question of authorial share that the century kept asking about its monument-building poets.
attribution_notes: Collaborative: Pope declared that some books were translated by other hands under his direction, and modern scholarship continues to argue the extent of the assistants' share, of William Brookes's revision and of Pope's own later versification.
bibliographical_notes: Published in volumes with separate title-pages beginning in 1725 and collected the same year; the states differ in their notes and in the order of the preliminary dissertation.

title: The Dunciad
alternative_titles: The Dunciad: A Heroic Poem in Four Books
description: Pope's satiric epic of Dulness enthroned in London: a mock-heroic coronation, games of the poetasters and a prophecy of the triumph of ignorance, directed at the trade in bad books, at dull scholarship and at the writer's own enemies.
plot_or_argument: Dulness and her son transfer the seat of their empire to the British capital, where the poetasters and booksellers compete for her prizes; her dominion is extended over the theatre, the presses and the schools of the city and the universities, until the poem closes on the extinction of light and order in an universal sleep of mind.
narrative_structure: Four books of mock-epic action, with invocation, games, prophecy and descent, framing a personal catalogue of the poet's enemies inside a cosmology of cultural decay.
principal_characters: Dulness; her son; the poet; Lewis Theobald; Edmund Curll; the tribe of poetasters and booksellers
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet strained to the strongest cadences of English satire, with the heavy monosyllabic line for the progress of Dulness and the rapid couplet for the attack.
historical_context: Written in the years after the failure of the Scriblerian papers, the success of the Homer and the quarrels over the Shakespeare edition; the immediate provocation was the hack scholarship and the pirated and hostile publishing to which Pope's name had become a commodity.
literary_significance: It is the central English poem of cultural despair, transforming personal revenge into a philosophy of the decline of letters, and it fixed the figure of Dulness as the century's image of its own public.
attribution_notes: Uncontested as Pope's, though the first edition's title-page carried its jokes about translation and about the author's name; the personae are real contemporary writers and the identification of several remains a bibliographical problem.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1728 in four books; the Dunciad Variorum followed in 1729, and the last revision, which transfers the crown of Dulness from Theobald to Cibber and adds later matter, was issued in the early 1740s.

title: The Dunciad Variorum
alternative_titles: The Dunciad in Four Books, with the Notes of the Variorum Editors
description: The 1729 edition of the Dunciad encrusted with a forged critical apparatus: prolegomena, the scholia of ancient and modern commentators, the key, the dedication to a living bookseller and the printed fragments of its enemies' works.
plot_or_argument: The same four books of the Dunciad are presented as an authenticated classic, annotated as if by a succession of editors and illustrated by the reprinted titles and offences of the dulness under attack.
narrative_structure: A satiric text inside a mock-scholarly frame: prolegomena, argument, notes in the manner of the classical editors, and appended documentary specimens of the offenders.
principal_characters: Dulness; the poet; the editor-personae of the apparatus; Lewis Theobald; Edmund Curll
literary_form: mock-scholarly satire in verse with apparatus
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet for the poem; the prose of the notes imitates the learned commentary, with Latin and Greek tags turned to burlesque.
historical_context: Made in the year of the quarrel over Shakespeare, when Theobald's restoration of the text had exposed Pope's own edition, and in the season of the booksellers' counter-publication of keys and replies.
literary_significance: Its invention of the hostile editorial apparatus turned scholarship itself into a satiric object and remains the period's most complete exposure of literary authority as a made thing.
attribution_notes: Collaborative: the notes and apparatus are the work of Pope's Scribleran circle, standardly credited in part to Arbuthnot and to other friends, and are spoken in the personae of invented editors rather than in Pope's own name.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1729 under the mask of various editors and with the engraved frontispiece; the text differs from the 1728 first edition in a number of lines and in the appended pieces.

title: Peri Bathous, the Art of Sinking in Poetry
alternative_titles: Peri Bathous: Or the Art of Sinking in Poetry
description: The Scribleran mock-technical treatise burlesquing the pseudo-Longinian essay on the sublime by codifying the art of the bathos: rules, instances and cautions for lowering the dignity of verse, with a chapter on the deeper and higher dulness.
plot_or_argument: An index of the figures and diseases of dull writing, delivered as a formal treatise with rules and examples: how to sink from sublimity, how to confound metaphor, and how the greater and lesser depths of bathos are to be measured.
narrative_structure: A mock-dissertation in numbered chapters and rules, prefixed to and commenting on the Dunciad's account of degenerate taste.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the academic index, with the definition, the division and the quoted example; the illustrations are verse specimens of failure.
historical_context: Circulated in the Scriblerus club papers of the second decade of the century and printed for the first time with the Dunciad Variorum, in the argument about taste, sublimity and the decline of poetry then being fought over Milton, over the unities and over the opera.
literary_significance: It supplied the century's word for the anticlimax of style and turned the technology of the treatise into a weapon, defining the sublime by its parody.
attribution_notes: Collaborative and disputed: a Scribleran compound circulated among Pope, Swift, Arbuthnot, Parnell and Atterbury, of which no separate contemporary edition exists and whose shares cannot be assigned; Pope printed it among his own apparatus without claiming its whole composition.
bibliographical_notes: First printed as one of the pieces annexed to the Dunciad Variorum in 1729; earlier states survive in club and miscellany manuscripts, and the text was reprinted in the miscellaneous collections of the circle.

title: An Essay on Man
alternative_titles: An Essay on Man in Four Epistles
Of the Nature and State of Man with Respect to the Universe
description: Pope's philosophical theodicy in four epistles, arguing that man's proper study is himself and his station in a graded creation, that what appears as evil in the part is good in the whole, and that self-love and social love are the same principle rightly directed.
plot_or_argument: Epistle I measures human knowledge against the immensity of the system and condemns presumption; II examines man's state as the middle creature of the chain of being; III argues that providence orders the passions to good ends; IV closes with the identity of interest and virtue and the sufficiency of happiness to the present life.
narrative_structure: Four numbered epistles in verse, each an continuous argument of proposition, instance and correction rather than narrative.
principal_characters: the poet-arguer; the friend addressed; the deist and the sceptic as imagined opponents
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet at its most gnomic and compressed, with the balanced pair, the interrogative sententia and the abrupt closing maxim.
historical_context: Written largely within the circle of St John, Viscount Bolingbroke, whose philosophy of nature it popularised, and published in the year of the deist and moral-philosophy controversies which drew the replies of Butler and of the clergy; its claim that whatever is, is right became a byword for optimism and its target for the satire of the following generation.
literary_significance: It was the most read English philosophical poem of the century, translating the Leibnizian and Shaftesburian theodicy into a schoolbook style, and drawing a century of attack from Kantian and romantic critics who thought its optimism a sophistry.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though its dependence on Bolingbroke's prose philosophy has made its originality a long-standing question.
bibliographical_notes: The several epistles were printed separately in 1732-33 and were collected in 1733-34; the text was revised under the eye of Warburton for the edition of the mid-1730s, and Blackmore publicly charged the poem with being borrowed from his own Creation.

title: Moral Essays
description: Pope's sequence of verse epistles on the characters of men and of women, on taste and on the use of riches: a social anatomy conducted in the manner of Theophrastus and of the periodical character writing.
plot_or_argument: Successive epistles examine the masks of the world, the inconstancy of female character, the false and the right use of wealth and the taste of the patron, and conclude that the science of life is the knowledge of ourselves.
narrative_structure: Four independent epistles, each opening on a general proposition, running through a gallery of portraits and closing with a moral reflection.
principal_characters: the poet-observer; the man of the world; the woman of fashion; the patron of taste; the rich man and his steward
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet of epigrammatic compression, with the rapid named portrait and the antithetical clause.
historical_context: Issued in the same years as the Essay on Man and the Horace imitations, when the character of women had become a pamphlet subject and when the language of taste and of the arts of the patron was being argued over Burlington's building and gardening.
literary_significance: It carries the periodical essay's moral taxonomy into verse and preserves the century's shrewdest and most contested analysis of character, wealth and national taste.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the satiric portraits are drawn from living persons whose identification has never been settled.
bibliographical_notes: The epistles were printed separately over several years and first gathered in a collected form in the middle of the decade; their order and their dedications vary between the states of the text, and the date of the epistle on female character is given here only as approximate.

title: The Imitations of Horace
description: Pope's free translations of Horace's satires and familiar epistles, in which the Roman poet's circle becomes the poet's own: a sequence of personated self-defence, retirement and judgment on the age.
plot_or_argument: Taking one Horatian poem after another, the speaker reports his own life among his friends and patrons, answers his enemies, refuses the offers of the great, and turns the ancient dialogue into an account of the modern writer's independence.
narrative_structure: A serial of separately printed imitations, each a self-contained dialogue or epistle, accumulating by recurrence of persons into an autobiography.
principal_characters: Horace as the personated speaker; Pope; the friend; the patron; the importunate poetaster; the bookseller
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet made colloquial and broken by the dialogue line, the interruption and the narrative aside, in deliberate contrast to the close cadence of the Essay on Criticism.
historical_context: Written across the later 1730s, after the failure of the last Scriblerian projects and in the years when the Licensing Act and the defeat of the administration changed the relation of the writer to party and patronage; Horace supplied the model of a private friendship publicly defended.
literary_significance: It redefined imitation as a modern mode of citation and self-portraiture, and it is the century's fullest demonstration that the ancients could be occupied rather than copied.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the mask of Horace is a deliberate prosopopoeia and the identification of the speakers with Pope's own circle has encouraged, without proving, division of hands in the earliest pieces.
bibliographical_notes: The imitations appeared separately between 1733 and 1738, some first in the newspapers, and were collected in Pope's own lifetime; ordering differs among the editions.

title: An Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot
description: Pope's apologia pro vita sua in couplets, addressed to his friend the physician John Arbuthnot: an account of the poet's peacable retirement, his parents, his enemies' persecution and the proper use of satire.
plot_or_argument: The epistle answers the pestering of the importunate poetaster, defends the poet's education and his independence, then reviews the masks of his attackers and ends by committing his cause to the candid reader and to his friend's judgment.
narrative_structure: A single verse epistle of argument and gallery, opening with the visitation scene, passing through the catalogue of offended persons, and closing on the valedictory portrait of the retired poet.
principal_characters: Dr Arbuthnot; the poet; Atticus; Sappho; Bavius; Mola; the importunate poetaster
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet of extraordinary conversational energy, with the interrupted address, the quoted opponent and the closing lapidary pair.
historical_context: Written in the season of the Horace imitations and of the quarrels over the Dunciad's enemies, when Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's verse attacks and the reviews of the poet's Homer had made personal satire a public business.
literary_significance: It is the century's most complete statement of the professional writer's defence of himself, and its personae, Atticus and Sappho above all, became the standard masks for the criticism of literary celebrity.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the identification of Atticus with Addison and of Sappho with Lady Mary Wortley Montagu is long established, though a few minor masks remain debated.
bibliographical_notes: First printed separately in 1735 and reprinted in the collected poems; the text was revised in the later editions of Pope's lifetime.

title: A Tale of a Tub
alternative_titles: A Tale of a Tub: Written for the Universal Improvement of Mankind
description: Swift's first great prose satire: the ironised digressions of a mad Grub Street author, within which the parable of the three brothers and their coats exposes the corruptions of the Christian churches, and which ends in the celestial voyage and the tower of Fame.
plot_or_argument: Three brothers, Peter, Martin and Jack, receive coats and a will from their father; Peter enlarges his coat with additions of his own, breaks the will and expels his brothers, so that Martin reforms and Jack splits into sects; the narrator's account of his own mechanical digressions and of the voyage to the island of the Aeolians surrounds the parable with a anatomy of enthusiasm, criticism and learning.
narrative_structure: A framed and digressive prose satire: the allegorical history of the brothers set within the narrator's self-revealing preface, digressions, mechanical project and voyage, with no continuous sequence of action.
principal_characters: Peter; Martin; Jack; the digressive narrator; the father; the mob of Grub Street
meter_and_prosody: Prose that passes from the nakedness of the plain style to the inflated cadences of the enthusiasm and the projectors, the satire carried by the register rather than by verse.
historical_context: Composed in the aftermath of the 1690s quarrel of the ancients and moderns and of the Toleration debate, and printed in 1704 with The Battle of the Books; its anticlerical edge long obstructed Swift's preferment, and he disowned its authorship when the volume was reissued at the height of the party war.
literary_significance: It founded the Swiftian method of complete impersonation of a deranged narrator and remains the century's most radical analysis of religious zeal, textual corruption and the pathology of printed learning.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Swift on the evidence of his friends and of the volume's later apparatus; Swift himself for long refused to own the book, and the ascription of individual passages of the appended pieces to his hand is debated.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1704 together with The Battle of the Books under the title-page claim of a fifth edition; the appended Designs of the Author and the further apparatus belong to the early editions of the second decade, and the several issues differ in their advertisements.

title: The Battle of the Books
alternative_titles: The Battle of the Books: A Paper, which was Read in a Great Club
description: Swift's short ironic allegory of the quarrel of the ancients and the moderns, in which the spider and the bee dispute over their claims to invention and to the honey of the hive, and the modern critick is defeated in the library of St James's.
plot_or_argument: The narrator enters the court library at the moment when the ancient and modern books fall out; the spider, who spins all things from his own bowels, and the bee, who gathers from abroad and digests what it collects, plead their rival causes, and the battle of the ants, the wasp and the critick ends with the ancient party's discomfiture and a joke at the author's expense.
narrative_structure: A brief narrative frame containing an allegorical dispute and a battle piece, closed by an authorial rebuke to the reporter.
principal_characters: the spider; the bee; the wasp; the critick; the narrator who reports the scene
meter_and_prosody: Plain Swiftian prose of the fable and the character, with the balanced pleading of the two rivals and the abrupt deflating close.
historical_context: Written in the season of Wotton's and Bentley's engagement over the quality of modern learning and of Temple's essay on ancient and modern discipline, and printed with the Tale of a Tub in 1704; it is the founding document of the Scribleran war against the modern critick.
literary_significance: It fixed the image of the two kinds of writer, the spider and the bee, and turned the rules-of-art quarrel into a durable piece of English literary mythology.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the piece was long circulated in manuscript before its 1704 printing.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1704 with the Tale of a Tub, where the title-page states that it had been longer written than the Tale and refers to a supposed earlier author; the separate issues of the two texts vary in their preface matter.

title: An Argument against Abolishing Christianity
alternative_titles: An Argument to Prove that the Abolishing of Christianity in England May Answer as Effectual to the Intended Ends as an Act of Indemnity
description: Swift's ironised pamphlet, spoken by a profession-deist who argues that Christianity should be quietly abolished because it is the source of all the nation's divisions, debt and enthusiasm, and that the nominal believers have nothing to lose.
plot_or_argument: The speaker enumerates the factions of the nominal Christians, the Whig deists, the fanatics and the heathen projectors, and urges that the name of Christ be removed from the currency, the liturgy and the oaths; the satire turns on the fact that the abolition he describes is already what the age's irreligion wants.
narrative_structure: A single continuous ironical argument, in the order of a speech or pamphlet, with enumerated categories of opponents and a closing peroration of apparent advice.
principal_characters: the profession-deist speaker; the nominal Christians; the heathen and deist projectors
meter_and_prosody: The dry prose of the parliamentary argument, with the accumulating catalogue and the flat declarative close.
historical_context: Written at the height of the deist and blasphemy controversies that followed the Toleration, and long held to have been intended for The Examiner; it was first printed in 1711 in the miscellaneous volumes that gathered Swift's tracts.
literary_significance: It is the sharpest short example of Swift's method of arguing in the voice of the enemy, and its diagnosis of a Christianity reduced to a party name made it a permanent scandal in the debate on toleration and irreligion.
attribution_notes: Uncontested as Swift's, though it was published anonymously and its first printing was not authorised under his name.
bibliographical_notes: The tract was circulated in manuscript and first printed in 1711; the occasion and the date of composition rest on internal evidence and on Swift's correspondence, and are given here only approximately.

title: The Predictions for the Year 1708 (Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.)
description: The astrological prediction sent in the name of Isaac Bickerstaff Esq. to a London almanack paper, foretelling with exact dates the death of the prognosticator John Partridge and other events of the year; the first move in the most successful practical joke of the century's print war.
plot_or_argument: Bickerstaff announces that he has corrected the almanack makers' errors and predicts Partridge's death on a specified day, together with the fate of several other prophets of the pressure of the times; the ensuing accounts of the accomplishment and the vindication of Bickerstaff carry the imposture into the newspapers.
narrative_structure: A short prediction tract followed by its pretended fulfilment and by the replies; the pieces form a single serial hoax conducted in the news sheets.
principal_characters: Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.; John Partridge the almanack maker; the rival prophets of the year
meter_and_prosody: The aphoristic future tense of the prognostication, in the manner of the old almanack verses, with the mock-profound numerical date.
historical_context: Published in the season of the Sacheverell ferment, when the party almanacks and the astrology of the press were instruments of political prediction; the trick drew Partridge's almanack for 1708 out of the market and gave Steele the paper mask he soon adopted.
literary_significance: It demonstrated the credibility of the press as a machine that could be fooled by its own conventions, and it created the Bickerstaff persona through which the Tatler and the Spectator would speak.
attribution_notes: Swift's authorship of the Bickerstaff papers is agreed, with a share in the later management of the hoax belonging to Steele, who wrote as Partridge's opponent and who inherited the mask.
bibliographical_notes: The prediction was put about at the end of 1707 and its supposed accomplishment printed in the spring of 1708, with several following pieces; the sequence was reprinted in the collected tracts, and the several impressions of the news sheets vary.

title: A Project for the Advancement of Learning
alternative_titles: A Project for the Advancement of Learning, and an Discourse of the Mechanical Operation of the Spirit
description: Swift's mock-project pamphlet, spoken by the same mad author of the Tale, which proposes that all learning may be bought at a shop and dispatched by mechanical means, and that the spirit of the age may be operated upon by instruments.
plot_or_argument: The projector offers the universities a compendium of the whole corpus of knowledge, abridged to a single pocket volume, together with the machinery of memorising, speaking and writing by art, and reports the cold reception of such projects by the learned.
narrative_structure: A continuous ironical proposal, in the manner of the machine pamphlets, with the narrator's narrative of his own failure appended.
principal_characters: the projector narrator; the universities and the learned societies; the mechanical authors
meter_and_prosody: The officious prose of the projector, full of article, offer and specification, broken by the narrator's self-pity.
historical_context: Written in the wake of the Tale and printed with the miscellaneous Swift pieces of 1711, in the season of the Royal Society's projects, the abridgement vogue and the new market for the mechanical digressions of learning.
literary_significance: It is the period's most economical exposure of the idea that knowledge can be mechanised, and it supplies the link between the Tale and the Laputa of the third book of Gulliver.
attribution_notes: Uncontested as Swift's; the piece belongs to the narrator of the Tale, so that the projected voice is a fiction rather than a statement of Swift's own educational program.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1711, in the volumes that gathered the Tale and its apparatus; some copies issue it with the Discourse of the Mechanical Operation of the Spirit and the priority of the several impressions is not settled.

title: The Conduct of the Allies
alternative_titles: The Conduct of the Allies: And of the Late Negotiation for a General Peace
description: Swift's great party pamphlet against the management of the War of the Spanish Succession, arguing that the confederate allies have made the war a business of conquest and that Britain's blood and treasure have been spent to the profit of the captains and the ministers.
plot_or_argument: The essay reviews the design of the Grand Alliance, the declarations and the campaigns, and shows by the allies' own papers how the nation was drawn into an endless war, before turning on the general and his ministers, whose conduct is figured as the picture of a great white animal of prey.
narrative_structure: A sustained historical argument in numbered parts, with the review of documents, the computation of the war's charges and the closing personal portrait.
principal_characters: the allies and their courts; the captains of the confederacy; the British ministry; the nation as the injured party
meter_and_prosody: The plain, emphatic prose of Swift's party writing, built from quotation, interrogative rebuke and the closing single sentence.
historical_context: Published in the winter of the ministerial change and the negotiation of the peace, at the height of the campaign to discredit the Duke of Marlborough and the Whig management, and repeatedly reprinted within the year as an instrument of the election and the address.
literary_significance: It is the most effective war pamphlet in English and a permanent document of the literature of anti-war argument, influencing the language in which the cost of campaigns and the credibility of ministers were questioned for two centuries.
attribution_notes: Swift's authorship has been occasionally queried by those who emphasised the ministry's hand in the pamphlet's publication, but it is now standardly assigned to him; the material he used was supplied from official sources.
bibliographical_notes: Many issues appeared in 1711 and 1712 with altered titles and added pieces, and the text was later incorporated in the collected Miscellanies; the several impressions differ in the prefatory letters.

title: The Examiner Papers
description: The thrice-weekly ministerial paper which Swift took over and turned into the ablest organ of Harley's peace administration: a sequence of party essays examining the Whig conduct of the war, the church in danger and the state of the nation.
plot_or_argument: The examiner reviews the party in office, the dissenters, the moneyed interest and the allies, and examines the arguments of the opposing papers, closing with the defence of the negotiation for the peace.
narrative_structure: Serial numbered papers, each a self-contained argument, with the occasional re-print of an opposing text for examination.
principal_characters: the Examiner as the speaking editor; the ministry in office; the dissenting clergy; the confederate allies
meter_and_prosody: Swift's bare and forceful prose style, the short closing sentence and the rhetorical question, in deliberate contrast to the periodic manner of the essay papers.
historical_context: The paper ran through the winter of the peace negotiation and the trial of the Sacheverell cause, and was conducted by Swift from about the autumn of 1710; Addison's Spectator was in part a reply to its method, and the contest of the two papers defined the political middle.
literary_significance: It marks the moment at which periodical prose became the chief weapon of English party politics, and it is Swift's school of the ironical examination that Gulliver and the Drapier later extend.
attribution_notes: Collaborative: the paper before Swift's direction and several numbers around him belong to other hands, and the division between Swift's papers and those of the associated writers remains a matter of bibliographical argument.
bibliographical_notes: Numbers appeared from 1710 to the middle of 1711 and were collected in volume form with the paper's replies; the numbering and the ascriptions of the collected volumes have been revised by modern editors.

title: A Proposal for Correcting, Improving and Ascertaining the English Tongue
alternative_titles: A Proposal for Correcting the English Tongue
description: Swift's plea for the regulation of English by public authority: a historical account of the language's corruption, a proposal for an academy of six or twelve persons to compile a dictionary, refine the tongue and ascertain its settled use.
plot_or_argument: The letter traces English from its Teutonick and Norman stocks, complains of the corruption introduced at the court of the late reign and by the politeness and the trade of the age, then argues that the language wants the authority of an academy, and offers a sketch of its rules and of the composition of a dictionary.
narrative_structure: A single letter, dividing into the historical complaint and the project, with the closing enumeration of the academy's methods.
meter_and_prosody: Swift's plain prose of the argument, with the historical enumeration and the abstract of the proposed rules.
historical_context: Written in the season of Addison's and Steele's attempt to polish English for the tea-table and to fix the idiom by authority, and addressed to the minister, in the years when the Royal Society's linguistic schemes and the project of an English academy were live topics.
literary_significance: It is the century's most influential statement of the desire to ascertain the language, and the direct provocation to the lexical and Augustan work which Johnson later performed without an academy.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1712 in the pamphlet that also carries the letter on the Earl of Oxford's ministry, and reprinted in the collected works; the order of the two letters varies between the states.

title: The Drapier's Letters
alternative_titles: Letters Written by M. B. Drapier to the People of Ireland
description: Swift's six letters to the people of Ireland against Wood's patent for a copper coinage, spoken in the plain voice of a wool-draper, and turning a monetary grievance into an argument about the rights of a dependent kingdom.
plot_or_argument: M. B. Drapier explains why the halfpence will ruin the kingdom's trade, answers the government's advocates and the friendly advisers who tell the people to submit, and rises in the later letters to the claim that a nation cheated of its own coin is being made a province of a project.
narrative_structure: A serial of open letters, each answering the previous objection, moving from the arithmetic of the coinage to the constitutional argument and to the invitation to resist.
principal_characters: M. B. Drapier; William Wood and his patent; the officers of the administration; the shopkeepers and weavers of Dublin
meter_and_prosody: The blunt idiom of the shopkeeper turned to oratory, with the plain short sentence, the repeated address to the people and the closing biblical tags.
historical_context: Published in Dublin in the year of Wood's patent, when the Irish currency question became the occasion for the first mass popular mobilisation against the administration, and when Swift's own station as dean of St Patrick's set him against the government his church depended on.
literary_significance: It made the language of liberty and of national resistance available to a dependent kingdom, and it is the century's most powerful instance of pamphlet writing changing the terms of an imperial quarrel.
attribution_notes: Swift's authorship, though long disavowed and pursued by the administration with a reward for the writer's discovery, is uncontested; the earlier answers printed against the letters include pieces by Irish writers and by Swift himself in another character.
bibliographical_notes: The letters appeared in Dublin in 1724 and were reprinted with the replies, the fourth letter with the Drapier's answer to the government's address; the collected edition of the letters with the associated tracts dates from later in the decade.

title: Gulliver's Travels
alternative_titles: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World
description: Swift's four-part voyage satire, narrated by the surgeon and captain Lemuel Gulliver, which reduces the scale of mankind to Lilliput, enlarges it in Brobdingnag, sends him to the flying island and the projectors of the Academy, and ends among the Houyhnhnms and the Yahoos.
plot_or_argument: Gulliver is cast away and reaches a nation of six-inch men whose politics, war and parties are a miniature of Europe; then a land of giants where his own species is judged; then the projects of the mechanicks and the shades of the dead; and finally a country of rational horses whose human brutes, the Yahoos, force him to see his own kind as vermin, till his return and his disgust.
narrative_structure: Four independent voyages in the first person, in the plain manner of the travel relation, each with its own ascent from curiosity to judgment; the sequence tightens from the political satire of the first two to the philosophical conclusion of the fourth.
principal_characters: Lemuel Gulliver; the court and army of Lilliput; the farmer and the queen of Brobdingnag; the sages of the flying island; the Houyhnhnms; the Yahoos
meter_and_prosody: The deliberately unadorned prose of the navigator's log, with the exact measurement, the enumeration of customs and the flat statement of the most outrageous conclusion.
historical_context: Written in the years between the fall of the Harley ministry and Swift's retirement to Dublin, and published anonymously in 1726 at a moment when the travel narrative and the new fiction of Defoe were making the invented first person respectable; the contemporary key identified nearly every personage of the first part.
literary_significance: It is the century's largest satiric fiction, converting the travellers' tale into an anatomy of human pride, and it founded the tradition of the constructed utopian and satirical voyage that runs to the nineteenth century.
attribution_notes: Published as the work of Lemuel Gulliver, initially a surgeon and lately a captain, with the printer's pretence of an unauthorised copy; Swift's authorship was understood at once and is uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in one volume in 1726 with the four parts complete; the text was revised for the collected edition of Swift's works in the middle of the following decade, and the several impressions differ in the preface and the corrections.

title: A Modest Proposal
alternative_titles: A Modest Proposal for Preventing the Children of Poor People from Being a Burthen to Their Parents or Country
description: Swift's ironical project for Ireland, in which a compassionate calculator proposes that the children of the poor be fattened and sold as food, and computes the profit to the landlord, the shopkeeper and the kingdom.
plot_or_argument: The projector states the misery of the breeders in Dublin, dismisses the expedients of others, then lays down the arithmetic of the infants' carcases, their skins and their use for the tables of the rich, and closes by listing the objections he has already answered.
narrative_structure: A single short tract in the form of a disinterested proposal, moving from the statement of the pressure, through the computation, to the catalogue of the scheme's additional advantages.
principal_characters: the projector; the knowing American of his acquaintance; the poor breeders and their children; the landlords and the shopkeepers
meter_and_prosody: The smooth arithmetical prose of political arithmetic, with the parenthesis of tender feeling and the exact figures of the computation.
historical_context: Printed in the depth of the Irish distress after the failure of the linen trade and the abortive schemes for the kingdom, when the pamphlets of political economy were proposing population and export as the remedy for poverty.
literary_significance: It is the most quoted single satire in English and the permanent example of what the ironised first person can do to a society's moral arithmetic, especially its calculation of human bodies as commerce.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the tract appeared anonymously with a fabricated Irish imprint in its first issue.
bibliographical_notes: First printed late in 1729 as a small pamphlet carrying a supposed foreign imprint; it was rapidly reprinted and was afterwards gathered into the collected Miscellanies.

title: Verses on the Death of Dr. Swift
alternative_titles: Verses Written at the Approach of His Death
description: Swift's poem on his own approaching death, written a decade before it and spoken from the sick chamber: a satiric inventory of the mourners, the friends, the flatterers and the enemies who will attend the funeral of the Dean of St Patrick's.
plot_or_argument: The dying speaker asks his friends to stop lamenting and permits the poem to rehearse the company of the wake, the visitors who will come to see the great man's end, the enemies who will rejoice, and the character of the Irish who have profited by him; it closes with the epitaph of the stern resting place.
narrative_structure: A single first-person meditation and catalogue, with the imagined future scenes of the mourning and the character of the nation interposed before the epitaph.
principal_characters: the dying Dean; his friends and visitors; his flatterers and his enemies; the people of Ireland
literary_form: satiric verse meditation on the self
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet of the plainest Swiftian hardness, with the run-over line and the abrupt maxim, deliberately unsentimental.
historical_context: Written in the year of the Dean's serious illness and of the Drapier triumph, when Swift's fame in Ireland was at its height and his English reputation had long been attached to the fallen ministry.
literary_significance: It is the century's hardest poem about dying and about the use of a reputation, the counterweight to the century's own cult of the funeral and the mourning poem.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the poem circulated in manuscript among Swift's friends before printing, and the copies differ in the order of the passages.
bibliographical_notes: Composition is dated by Swift's own use of the year 1731; the first printing is generally assigned to the middle of the following decade and the priority of the copies is not settled, so the publication date is given here only approximately.

title: The Legion Club
description: Swift's last great verse satire, directed against a Dublin club of the Whig and court interest and against the Irish legislature it feeds, in which the poet's Muse is pressed into an inventory of the age's knaves and fools.
plot_or_argument: The poet, appealed to by his Muse to name the wickedness of the times, enumerates the members and the purposes of the Legion Club, the lawyers, the informers and the patriots of the kingdom's administration, and discharges his subject in a catalogue of abuse.
narrative_structure: A dialogue frame with the Muse opening, followed by an accumulating catalogue and a closing dismissal.
principal_characters: the poet; the Muse; the members of the club; the managers of the Irish parliament
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet driven at speed, with the reiterate name and the heaped epithet, the most violently colloquial of Swift's verse.
historical_context: Written in the years when the Irish administration and the Whig clubs of Dublin had set Swift against the establishment of the kingdom he had defended in the Drapier's letters, and suppressed on publication when the Dublin printer was prosecuted.
literary_significance: It is the ferocious close of Swift's satiric career and a permanent record of what verse invective could do to a party, and its suppression made it one of the century's notable cases of the writer against the licensing power.
attribution_notes: Uncontested as Swift's; published without his name, and the copies were largely destroyed by the prosecution.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Dublin in 1737 and immediately pursued; the text survived in the few copies and in reprints, and was first gathered into the collected works after Swift's death.

title: Trivia
alternative_titles: Trivia; or, the Art of Walking the Streets of London
description: Gay's mock-didactic guide to the sights, shows, coaches, clothes and night entertainments of London, written as an art of town-walking in the manner of the classical didactic poem.
plot_or_argument: The Muse of Trivia instructs the citizen and the country visitor where to look and how to dress, what to see by day in the parks, the exchange and the shops, and what to seek by night in the tavern, the box at the theatre and the masquerade, with an antiquarian appendix on the town's own history.
narrative_structure: Three books of didactic argument after the manner of the art poem, with the catalogue of places and the closing historical inquiry.
principal_characters: the poet and his Muse of Trivia; the town of London and its shows
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet of easy narrative breadth, with the rapid list and the colloquial tag.
historical_context: Published in the season of the Spectator's town-painting essays and of the new London guide books, when the coach, the pawn and the opera made the street a subject of moral and commercial description.
literary_significance: It is the century's most charming urban descriptive poem and the complement to the country prospect of Windsor-Forest, preserving the topology of Augustan London for later readers.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the poem appeared among the pieces of a periodical miscellany conducted by Gay and his friends, which has encouraged occasional mis-division of the volume's parts.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1716 in octavo with the dedication and the additional notes; later issues gather the poem with the Shepherd's Week and the shorter verse.

title: The Shepherd's Week
alternative_titles: The Shepherd's Week, in Seven Days
description: Gay's burlesque pastoral of the seven days of a labouring week, in which the lovelorn swains of the conventional eclogue are replaced by clowns, ale, the wake, the farthing spit and the spilling of the dish of milk.
plot_or_argument: Pastoral courtship, complaint and banquet are enacted by village swains in their real occupations, and the week closes with the plainest of love matches; the ancient machinery and the fine phrases of the eclogue are retained only to be laughed at.
narrative_structure: Seven day-poems, each on one pastoral action, with the introductory preface and the explanatory notes defending the low imitation.
principal_characters: the clowns and shepherd swains of the week; the shepherdesses of the courtship plots
