meter_and_prosody: Varied stanzaic imitation of the old pastoral and of Spenser, in short lines and plain diction, with the deliberate bathos of the closing couplet.
historical_context: Published in the year of the quarrel over pastoral diction, when Pope's Pastorals and Philips's own eclogues had made the representation of real shepherds a critical issue; the volume's prose preface and notes are part of the same argument.
literary_significance: It broke the genteel pastoral and opened the way for the rustic and labouring representation of country life that the later century inherited, and it supplied the burlesque method Gay himself carried to the stage a dozen years later.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1714 and reissued in a corrected second edition the same year with the preface and the notes; it was subsequently gathered into the collected poems issued by subscription.

title: What D'Ye Call It
alternative_titles: What D'Ye Call It: A Comedy
description: Gay's comic burlesque of the modern drama, which plays heroic tragedy, the sentimental plot and the new French manner against one another and asks the audience by what name the stage-piece is to be called.
plot_or_argument: A country family and a pair of lovers are involved in an outrageously regular tragedy of captive princes, recognition and virtue rewarded, until the housemaid's dream and the exposures of the plot turn the whole into farce; the play ends by denying that it belongs to any known species.
narrative_structure: Five acts of prose comedy with inserted scenes of rhymed heroic tragedy and a dream piece, the forms being parodied against each other.
principal_characters: the lovers of the burlesqued tragic plot; the country family; the dreaming housemaid; the critic of the audience
meter_and_prosody: Prose dialogue interrupted by heroic-couplet and blank-verse tragedy, the shift of metre carrying the satire.
historical_context: First acted in the season after the death of the queen and the change of ministry, when the pastiche of operatic and tragic convention was a competitive theatrical genre and when the theatre managers were anxious over the vogue for the old and the new. It answered the running of Addison's and Rowe's tragedies in the same houses.
literary_significance: It is one of the founding pieces of English dramatic burlesque and a direct preparation for the Beggar's Opera, and it records the century's argument about genre in the comic register.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in quarto in 1715 with the account of the performance; the several editions vary in the length of the tragic interpolations.

title: The Beggar's Opera
description: Gay's ballad opera, proposed by Pope as a burlesque of the Italian heroic opera, in which the highwayman, the thief-taker and the Newgate clerks are made to sing the airs of the town, and the criminal economy of the city is staged as the mirror of high life.
plot_or_argument: Macheath, the gay highwayman, is betrayed by Peachum to Lockit and to the gallows, having married both Polly and Lucy; the rival fathers scheme, the gang quarrels, and the last-minute reprieve, protested by the Beggar who superintends the piece, exposes the convention by which the hero of quality escapes the rope.
narrative_structure: An opera in three acts with spoken dialogue between the airs, framed by the Beggar's argument with the poet and the composer about probability and about the fate of the hero.
principal_characters: Macheath; Peachum; Lockit; Polly Peachum; Lucy Lockit; the gang; the Beggar; the Player
meter_and_prosody: Ballad and song stanzas of the street and the theatre, set to borrowed airs, alternating with prose dialogue; the metres are those of the popular tune rather than of the dramatic blank verse.
historical_context: First performed and printed in the season of the London opera companies' triumph with Handel's Italian dramas, and of the South Sea collapse, when the language of credit, the press gang and the property of the stage were all in dispute; the work was licensed without difficulty and became the most pirated text of the decade.
literary_significance: It created the ballad opera, made the criminal underworld the true subject of a musical entertainment, and remains the century's most sustained identification of the gallows and the drawing room as one economy.
attribution_notes: Gay's, on the plan suggested by Pope; the airs, the tunes and the many pirated keys and continuations are other men's work.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in quarto in 1728 and reprinted through that year with the second act's additional songs and with the tunes printed; the text of the first performance and of the later stage alterations differ.

title: Polly
alternative_titles: Polly: A Sequel to the Beggar's Opera
description: Gay's sequel to the Beggar's Opera, in which the reprieved Macheath, transported and escaped, pursues Polly to a plantation in the southern colonies, where she is disguised as a man and the slaves Cato and Lucida enact a tragedy of conjugal constancy.
plot_or_argument: Macheath, having cheated the gallows, is banished, escapes his creditors and the governor, and reaches the American planter's household; Polly follows in a man's dress, is assaulted in the dark by her own husband and by the land-jobber Mordecai's intrigue, and the play closes with the exposures of the lovers' fidelity, the refusal of the transport and the Beggar's renunciation of the sequel.
narrative_structure: Three acts of ballad opera with the plantation scenes and the inserted slave tragedy, framed by the Beggar's dispute with the writer of the sequel.
principal_characters: Polly; Macheath; Lucy Lockit; Mordecai the land-jobber; Cato and Lucida, slaves on the plantation; the governor of the province; the Beggar
meter_and_prosody: Air-songs in ballad and sentimental stanzas with borrowed tunes, and the elegiac measures of the inserted slave scenes.
historical_context: Written immediately after the success of the Beggar's Opera and forbidden by the Lord Chamberlain in the season of the administration's quarrel with the theatre, so that it reached the reading public in print rather than the stage; its colonial setting answers the plantation and transport literature of the same years.
literary_significance: It turns the burlesque of the first opera into a sharper analysis of credit, marriage, transport and slavery, and its suppression made it the century's standard instance of the political censorship of the stage.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the licence refused by the Lord Chamberlain is documented, and the sequel's later stage history is complex and is not asserted here.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by subscription in 1729 with the dedication and the preface on the stage; its first public performance is a matter of later-eighteenth-century accounts which this record does not date.

title: Fables (First Collection)
alternative_titles: Fables by John Gay, Part the First
description: Gay's first collection of the beast fables, cast in the manner of the Eastern and classical apologue and applied, in the dedication and the moral, to the court, the city, the stage and the marriage market of his own country.
plot_or_argument: A succession of short tales of beasts, birds and insects, each closing with an application: on credulity and the guide who leads the rash, on the great and their favourites, on the tyrant and his courtiers, on the traveller and the city, and on the marriage market.
narrative_structure: A collection in numbered books of independent fables, each with its own narrative and appended application, unified only by the dedicator's frame.
principal_characters: the beasts and birds of the apologues; the court, the city and the theatre they figure
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet in the plainest narrative use, with the short sententious close that carries the moral.
historical_context: Published by subscription in the year of the Beggar's Opera's first run, when the vogue for eastern tales and for La Fontaine's imitators had made the apologue a vehicle of national comment; the dedication commends the instruction of a princess of the House of Hanover.
literary_significance: It restored the fable to the English canon as a form of social and political realism, and it long stood in the schoolroom beside Aesop and later with the century's own collection of the short moral tale.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the collection reworks earlier apologue material, and Gay acknowledges his Eastern and classical obligations.
bibliographical_notes: First issued in 1727 in a subscription volume divided into three books; the count of the fables and the division into books vary a little among the issues, and the second collection followed eleven years later.

title: Fables (Second Collection)
alternative_titles: Fables by John Gay, Part the Second
description: Gay's second and last collection of fables, prepared for publication shortly before his death and more openly personal and political than the first, with the poet's own retirement and independence as its recurring subject.
plot_or_argument: Independent apologues of beasts, plants and the domesticks of the world, each with its application, several of them taking the fortunes of court friendship, the poet's patron and the dangers of the great.
narrative_structure: A collection in books of separate fables with their morals, framed by the poet's retirement among his books and closing with the fable of the old apple-tree.
principal_characters: the beasts and trees of the apologues; the court friend and the poet
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet, more reflective and sometimes more broken than in the first collection, with the lyric insertion in the closing fable.
historical_context: Composed across the 1730s, after the suppression of Polly and the withdrawal of the theatre patronage, and published in the year of Gay's death in the subscription manner he had used for the first collection.
literary_significance: It completes the most considerable English fable sequence of the century and preserves the image of the poet's protected retirement which the age attached to Gay's memory.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1738, with the two collections afterwards printed together; the order of several fables differs between the issues.

title: Poems on Several Occasions (Gay)
description: Gay's collected poems, gathered by subscription and bringing together Trivia, the Shepherd's Week and the occasional verse, epistles and burlesques of his first years in town.
plot_or_argument: The volume passes from the town's shows and the village week to the verse epistles to his friends, the lyric and the theatrical prologue, without sustained narrative argument.
narrative_structure: A collected miscellany arranged by piece rather than by design, with the dedication and the advertisements ordering the contents.
principal_characters: the poet and his friends; the town and the country of the earlier poems
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet for the didactic and epistolary pieces, and the lyric and mock-Spenserian stanzas for the shorter poems.
historical_context: Issued by subscription at the opening of the decade, when the country seat and the patron's list were the means by which a professional poet financed a volume; the subscription itself included the great names of the new architecture and of the court.
literary_significance: It fixed Gay's public reputation before the Beggar's Opera and shows the full range of the minor Augustan verse, from urban description to the fable and the epistle.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the collection reprints pieces first issued separately or in miscellanies, and the ordering is the author's.
bibliographical_notes: Published by subscription in 1720, the volume being the most profitable of its year; the later collected poems of the author reprint the pieces with the additions of the 1730s.

title: The Hermit
description: Parnell's tender narrative tale of a hermit drawn from his cell by a pleasing guide, of a betrayed country maid, and of the care exercised over the tempted soul: one of the most reprinted English short poems of the century.
plot_or_argument: An old hermit, peevish at the world and at his own past, is allured from his cell by a fair guide who leads him through the country night to a cottage, where he learns the story of a maid seduced and lost; the tale turns on the discovery of the guide's errand and on the hermit's humbling.
narrative_structure: A single romance tale in verse, with the inset narrative of the maid and a closing revelation.
principal_characters: the hermit; the guiding spirit; the seduced maid of the inset tale; the rural household
meter_and_prosody: Plain couplet and short lyric stanza of the old ballad manner, with the night description in a slower measure.
historical_context: Published in the years when the ballad, the romance tale and the tender religious narrative were displacing the heroic manner, and when Pope and the Scriblerans held Parnell's verse to be the model of easy native simplicity.
literary_significance: It supplied the century with one of its most quoted examples of pathos and of the supernatural tale, and its reprints, translations and schoolbook presence made it a conduit for the sentimental ballad.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Usually assigned to 1722 as a separate print; it appears in the collected poems of Parnell issued in the following years, and the priority of the several copies is not settled here.

title: Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
alternative_titles: An Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
description: Parnell's short verse essay on the styles proper to the several kinds of poetry, arguing that the numbers of verse must be chosen for the subject and that the harmony of the line is a matter of judgment rather than of rule.
plot_or_argument: The essay distinguishes the lofty, the smooth and the loose measures, censures the affectation of harmony for its own sake, and commends the poet who suits his stiles to his design.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in verse, opening with the occasion and closing in a character of the finished poet.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet, with the illustrative lines deliberately imitating the measures under discussion.
historical_context: Published in the years of the quarrel over rhyme, blank verse and the harmony of the couplet, when the periodical essay, Dennis's criticism and Pope's Essay on Criticism were making versification a public argument.
literary_significance: It is one of the earliest and most readable English poems on style and numbers, and it stands beside the Essay on Criticism for its account of imitation in verse.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the printing history of the piece is obscure and it survives chiefly in the collected editions of Parnell's poems.
bibliographical_notes: The date follows the standard modern accounts of Parnell's works; the first separate impression has not been verified for this record, and the composition dates are left null.

title: Creation, a Philosophical Poem
alternative_titles: Creation: A Philosophical Poem, Written in the Measure of Milton's Paradise Lost
description: Blackmore's physico-theological poem, which reads the frame of nature, the senses, the faculties of the mind and the order of the creation as evidence of one intelligent and benevolent Maker, and defends reason against enthusiasm and atheism.
plot_or_argument: The poem contemplates the chaos and the formation of the world, the parts of animals, the mechanisms of the senses and the passions, and the immateriality of the soul, drawing from each the argument for a Deity and for a moral order established in nature.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in numbered books, each a course of natural and philosophical reflection rising to a theological conclusion.
principal_characters: the poet-teacher; the Deity addressed; the mind of man as the spectacle
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic measure Blackmore claims on his title page, of a deliberate and often lumbering fullness.
historical_context: Written in the season of the Boyle lectures and of the vogue for the argument from the frame of nature, after Ray, Derham and the new mechanical philosophy had made the observation of the creatures a branch of natural religion.
literary_significance: It is the largest English attempt to put the physico-theological argument in Miltonic verse, and its quarrel with Pope over the originality of the Essay on Man makes it a document of the century's dispute about optimism.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1712 in the form then issued; the complete three books and the enlarged later issues were put out in the following decade, and the several editions differ in the argument and the notes.

title: Redemption
description: Blackmore's last large religious poem, a sacred epic of the redemption of mankind which carries the Miltonic measure of Creation into the history of the fall and the work of the Saviour.
plot_or_argument: The poem reviews the fall of man and the promise of redemption, the training of the Old Testament and the coming, teaching and passion of Christ, and closes on the application of the saving work to the conscience of the reader.
narrative_structure: A continuous sacred narrative in numbered books, with the theological reflection interposed in the poet's own voice.
principal_characters: the poet; the redeeming Saviour; Satan; the figures of the Old and New Testament narrative
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic manner, sustained through the longest of Blackmore's religious poems.
historical_context: Published in the closing years of the century's first great quarrel over the poem of religion, when Blackmore's verse had long been the target of the Scribleran burlesque of the art of sinking.
literary_significance: It completes the series by which the physico-theological and the sacred epic were attempted in Miltonic blank verse, and it documents the isolation of a once fashionable poet from the taste that had superseded him.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The date follows the standard modern accounts of Blackmore's epics; the full title-page wording, the number of books of the first issue and the composition dates could not be verified for this record and are given only approximately.

title: The Ambitious Stepmother
description: Rowe's first tragedy, a play of a Hellenistic court in which an ambitious stepmother's pursuit of her stepson and the struggle for a kingdom destroy one another; it made Rowe's reputation as the successor to the regular tragedy of the Restoration stage.
plot_or_argument: A king's second wife, inflamed with an unlawful passion for the son of his first bed, presses her claim and her desire until the conspiracies, the jealousies and the rival affections of the court end in discovery and death.
narrative_structure: Regular five-act tragedy of intrigue and recognition, with the passion of the stepmother as the governing mechanism of the plot.
principal_characters: the ambitious stepmother; the injured prince of the first bed; the king; the heroine of the court
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of the post-Dryden regularity, with the set rhetorical complaint and the sententious short line.
historical_context: Acted at the opening of the century by the company in which the actors of the Restoration tradition still controlled the patent houses, at the moment when the reformed regularity of French-model tragedy was being pressed against the heroic mode.
literary_significance: It established Rowe as the century's chief practitioner of moral and pathetic tragedy and marks the passage from the heroic drama of the 1670s to the regulated, sentimentally serious stage of the Augustans.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1700 and reissued with corrections in Rowe's lifetime and after; the names of the characters are given generically here because the several editions vary their spelling.

title: The Fair Penitent
description: Rowe's tragedy of Calista, a woman of quality betrayed into a private guilt which is discovered and judged: the most acted and most read English tragedy of the first half of the century, and the founding play of the pathetic drama of female frailty.
plot_or_argument: Calista, long yielded to the gay deceiver Altamonte and still engaged elsewhere, is exposed by the discovery of her correspondence; her father Sciolto pronounces and executes the family judgment, and the play closes in the deaths of the offenders and of the injured.
narrative_structure: Five acts of discovery and judgment, with the private correspondence as the mechanism of exposure and the father's sentence as the catastrophe.
principal_characters: Calista; Sciolto; Altamonte; Lavinia
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of sustained pathetic declamation, with the broken address and the long-completed sentence of the penitential speeches.
historical_context: Written for the players of the patent theatre in the years when the reformation of the stage was being argued in print, and long identified with the acting of the century's chief tragic actresses.
literary_significance: It made the betrayed and penitent woman the central pathetic figure of the English stage and supplied the plot and the vocabulary that the sentimental drama and the novel of seduction later prosified.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in quarto in 1703 and reissued frequently with the alterations of the playhouse; the dedicatory preface varies between the early issues.

title: Ulysses
alternative_titles: The Tragedy of Ulysses, King of Ithaca
description: Rowe's last completed tragedy, taking the return of Ulysses to a court and a household invaded by suitors, and making the trial of recognition and of constancy the moral centre of the play.
plot_or_argument: The disguised king of Ithaca watches the insolence of the suitors and the trial of his wife's fidelity, and the recognition of Ulysses by his son and his household issues in the destruction of the invaders and the restoration of order.
narrative_structure: Regular tragedy in five acts on the Homelian argument, organised as a progression from disguise and observation to recognition and judgment.
principal_characters: Ulysses; Penelope; Telemachus; the suitors of Ithaca
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of the later Rowe, plainer and more argumentative than that of The Fair Penitent, with the formal recitative of the recognitions.
historical_context: Acted at Drury Lane in the last season of Rowe's official connection with the theatre, in the years when the classical and Homerick subjects were being reworked for a public that was turning to the opera and the pantomime.
literary_significance: It closes the line of regular Augustan classical tragedy that Rowe had helped to establish, and its handling of fidelity and of the invaded household shows the moral drama of the Fair Penitent transferred to the Homerick subject.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1722 with the dedication and the prefatory account of the argument; the several issues differ in the length of the dumb show and the ceremonial scenes.

title: The Royal Convert
description: Rowe's tragedy of religion, conscience and political conversion in an early Northern court, in which a princess's change of faith entangles duty, affection and the succession.
plot_or_argument: A royal convert's new religion divides her family and her lover's allegiance, and the conspiracies raised about the throne, with the treachery of a waiting-woman substituted for the daughter, drive the play to its discoveries and executions.
narrative_structure: Five acts of court intrigue, with the recognition of the substituted woman as the plot's famous mechanism and the religious division as its motive force.
principal_characters: the royal convert; her lover and rival claimants; the substituted bride; the father of the house
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of the regular school, with the argumentative scene of conscience and the declaimed religious debate.
historical_context: Acted at Drury Lane in the season of the Occasional Conformity disputes, when the conscience of a convert and the loyalty of a subject were live political questions in England.
literary_significance: It is the century's earliest considerable tragedy of conscience and conversion, and its substitute-bride intrigue became one of the most imitated devices of the pathetic drama.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The date of the first edition and of the first performance is given from the playhouse and quarterly evidence and is approximate; the piece was reissued in the collected editions of Rowe's works, which alter the scene divisions.

title: Jane Shore
description: Rowe's tragedy of the mistress of Edward the Fourth, reduced from her court favour to penance and poverty: the most persistent example of the fallen woman's tragedy on the eighteenth-century stage.
plot_or_argument: Jane Shore, cast off with the king's death and pursued by the malice of Gloucester, abandons her riches, does public penance in the streets of London and dies in the humility of her own repentance, while the politics of the court and the fate of Hastings carry the action.
narrative_structure: Five acts of court history and private fall, with the public penance and the closing deathbed scene as the two calculated crises.
principal_characters: Jane Shore; King Edward the Fourth; Hastings; Gloucester; Alicia
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of a deliberate plainness, with the prose of the lower stations and the sententious couplet at the scene's close.
historical_context: Acted at Drury Lane in the last months of the reign and the season of the succession, when the mirror of princes and the fate of the king's mistress were transparently political subjects.
literary_significance: It fixed the penitent courtesan as a permanent figure of English moral drama and, with The Fair Penitent, established the female calamity plot that Richardson and the sentimental drama later inherited.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in quarto in 1714 and reprinted with the additions of the later issues; several editions carry prefatory matter on the historical mistress of Edward the Fourth.

title: Lucan's Pharsalia Translated
alternative_titles: Lucan's Pharsalia Translated into English Verse
description: Rowe's verse translation of Lucan's civil-war epic, the work by which the English reader of the early century knew the wars of Caesar and Pompey and the Stoic Cato.
plot_or_argument: The translation follows Lucan's argument of the breach between Caesar and Pompey, the flight from Rome, Pharsalia and the suicide of Cato, with the poet's own reflections on the loss of Roman liberty running through the narrative.
narrative_structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the ten books of the Pharsalia, with the preface, the arguments and the explanatory notes.
principal_characters: Caesar; Pompey; Cato; Lucan as the translated author
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet of the regular Augustan kind, straining to carry Lucan's declamation and his apostrophes.
historical_context: Published in the years when the republicanism and the liberty of the Roman commonwealth were being read into the quarrels of the British constitution, and when the translation of the classics had become a profession's work.
literary_significance: It was the standard English Lucan of the first half of the century, and its translator was later made the point of a satiric joke about the rendering that outdoes its original.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the volume's later issues were revised and part of the prefatory matter has been assigned to another hand.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1709 with the preface on the occasion of the translation and the notes on the sixth book; the format and the title-page wording of the first issue were not verified for this record, and the enlarged collected editions reprint the version with revisions.

title: Winter
description: The first of Thomson's seasonal poems: a description of the closing year, the frost, the snow and the thaw, in which the rigour of the weather tries the labouring poor and the mind of the spectator together.
plot_or_argument: The poem passes from the early frost and the wild fowl of the fen through the deep snow, the cottage fire-side, the sports of the frozen field and the house of labour, to the thaw and the drowning of the country, closing on the contemplation of death and of the season of the soul.
narrative_structure: A continuous descriptive progression through the phases of one season, animated by inset tales, the apostrophe to the personified mood of the opening, and the reflection addressed to the spectator.
principal_characters: the personified musing of the opening invocation; the peasant and the shepherd of the frozen country; the wild fowl of the fen; the hare, the stag and the huntsmen
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines of great period-length, with the suspended syntax, the accumulation of adjective and participle and the onomatopoeic weather passage.
historical_context: Published in the year after Thomson's arrival in London from the north, in the season when the lapse of licensing, the new topographical taste and the debate over the merits of blank verse made a long descriptive poem on the weather a commercial and critical event.
literary_significance: It renewed English descriptive verse by making weather and labour rather than estate and prospect the subject, and it gave the century the diction of natural observation that Cowper, Crabbe and Wordsworth later absorbed.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1726, reprinted with the addition of the pastoral and the reflection in the following years, and collected with the rest of the seasons in 1730; the poem was revised again in the later editions of Thomson's lifetime.

title: Summer
description: The second of Thomson's seasonal poems, carrying the reader from the morning of the ripening year through the heat, the storm and the evening coolness of summer, with the episode of the rural lovers and the poem on the grove and the hound.
plot_or_argument: The day and the weather of summer are traced from the early morning to the night, the labours of the hay field and the flock, the threat of the tempest and the relief of the cool, while the story of two lovers is interrupted and completed within the season's changes.
narrative_structure: A diurnal and meteorological progression, with the inset tale of the lovers and the hymn and ode passages interposed at the crisis of the storm.
principal_characters: the rural lovers of the inset tale; the labourers of the field; the storm and the evening
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines, with the long compound period for the advancing weather and the short lyric interlude for the hymn and the tale.
historical_context: Issued as a separate poem in the season of Thomson's patronage at Richmond, in the same years in which the natural-history writing and the new landscape taste were making the description of the growing year respectable.
literary_significance: Its storm passage and its treatment of the growing year are the most influential pieces of weather writing in English, and they established the seasonal structure that the later descriptive and meditative poems adopted.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1727 and collected with the rest in 1730; the poem was enlarged and altered in the later editions, and the several states differ in their lyrics and hymns.

title: Spring
description: The third of Thomson's seasonal poems, on the return of the year and on the love and generation it awakens, closing with the prospect of the human season and the hymn to the creator of the seasons.
plot_or_argument: The opening of the year is described in its birds, its blossoms and its gales, the song of the groves and the courtship of the creation; the poem then turns to the spring of human life, to love and to the education of the mind, and to the moral use of the season.
narrative_structure: A progressive description of the season's return, with the address to the poet's friend and the reflection on human youth interposed before the closing hymn.
principal_characters: the birds and the groves of the returning year; the friend addressed in the poem's second half; the human lovers of the spring
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines, with the short spring measures of the bird and flower passages and the stately period of the hymn.
historical_context: Published in the year of the quarrel over the opera and of the new topographical vogue, and the part of the sequence most deeply affected by Thomson's later rewriting in the middle of the century.
literary_significance: Its account of the returning year and of human youth became the common stock of English descriptive and lyrical writing, and its later state is the chief example of Thomson's revision of his own seasons.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1728 and collected in 1730; the poem was largely rewritten for the edition of the middle of the 1740s, and the two states of the text differ extensively.

title: Autumn
description: The fourth of Thomson's seasonal poems, on the harvest, the gleaning, the vine and the melancholy of the closing year, with the celebrated account of the poet's own love and the meditation on the season of the mind.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the year to its ripening and its ingathering, the harvest field, the orchard and the vineyard, the mists and the melancholy of the evening, and ends with the tale of Cynia and the poet's retreat to contemplation and to the hymn of the season.
narrative_structure: A descriptive progression through the operations of the harvest, with the inset love tale and the closing meditative retreat.
principal_characters: the reapers and the gleaners of the harvest field; the maid of the inset tale; the contemplative poet
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines of the most sustained richness in the sequence, with the long evening period and the inserted lyric ode.
historical_context: Issued at the close of the first publication of the four seasons, when the poem of the harvest and of melancholy was the most fashionable species of descriptive writing.
literary_significance: It gave English verse its enduring imagery of autumn, harvest and melancholy evening, and its meditation on the seasons of the mind is the direct ancestor of the mid-century night and graveyard poem.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The separate issue is generally assigned to 1728 and the poem was first gathered with the others in the collected Seasons of 1730; the priority of the separate print could not be independently verified for this record.

title: Liberty
alternative_titles: Liberty, a Poem, in Three Parts
description: Thomson's didactic poem on civil and moral liberty, in three parts: the ancient and modern history of free states, the constitution of Britain, and the relation of liberty to the arts, commerce and the sentiments of the individual.
plot_or_argument: The poet invokes Liberty and traces her causes and effects in commonwealths and in the British constitution, argues that trade and independence are the guardians of the state, and passes in the last part to the culture of the mind, the fine arts and the virtue which alone can preserve a free people.
narrative_structure: Three separately issued parts, each an argument of history, reflection and apostrophe, with the inserted episodes of the Swiss and Dutch deliverers and of the patriot.
principal_characters: the goddess Liberty invoked; the patriot and the statesman; the free commonwealths of the example
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of the seasonal manner, more declamatory and more sententious than the descriptive poems, with the apostrophic invocation.
historical_context: Published in the years of the patriot-Whig opposition to the Walpole administration, when the country language of liberty, independent property and the standing army was being renewed in poetry and in the journals.
literary_significance: It is the century's most ambitious attempt to make the history of free government the subject of a serious didactic poem, and it supplied the vocabulary of liberty later used by the American and the British radical traditions.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The parts appeared successively in 1734 and in the two following years, with the dedication and the argument varying between the issues; a fourth part was projected and is not treated here.

title: Britannia (Thomson)
description: Thomson's patriotic poem, calling on the national spirit and the naval force of the island and urging that Britain's safety lies in the command of the sea and in the virtue of a free people.
plot_or_argument: The poem summons the genius of the country, remembers its ancient and modern deliverances, and argues that the naval and commercial power of Britain is the instrument of her liberty against the ambition of the continent.
narrative_structure: A continuous patriotic argument in the ode-like measures of the anthem, with the historical recollection and the direct address to the nation.
principal_characters: the genius of Britannia; the navy and the merchant; the threatened nation
meter_and_prosody: The martial and anthem-like measures of the national ode, with the short stirring line and the recurring summons; the precise stanzaic scheme of the first issue is not asserted here.
historical_context: Written in the years of the disputes over the navy and the commercial system that preceded the war of the Spanish succession, when the government's pacific economy was being attacked by the patriot writers in the language of the island's sea power.
literary_significance: It is one of the founding texts of the British naval-patriotic lyric, the immediate context of the odes on the rule of the ocean which the following years made national.
attribution_notes: Disambiguated in the title from Camden's LATIN Britannia already in this database; the poem here is Thomson's.
bibliographical_notes: The poem is commonly held to have been composed early in the decade and withheld until its publication in 1737; the date of composition is therefore given here only approximately.

title: Alfred
description: Thomson's masque on Alfred the Great and the deliverance of the Saxon kingdom, written for the prince's country house and closed by the ode on the dominion of the sea which became the national song.
plot_or_argument: The young Alfred, nursed in exile and instructed in the history of his house, is restored against the Danish power by the counsel and the example of the ancient British worthies; the vision of the nation's future is disclosed to him, and the masque ends with the invocation of the ocean's rule.
narrative_structure: A masque in one act with the recitative, the chorus and the prophetic vision, closing in a separately numbered ode.
principal_characters: Alfred; the Saxon counsellors of the exile; the Danish power; the choruses of the British worthies
meter_and_prosody: Alternating recitative lines, the regular stanzas of the song and the anthem measure of the closing ode, written for composition.
historical_context: Prepared for the court of the Prince of Wales at his country seat, with music by the century's chief theatre composer, in the season when the patriot circle made the ancient British mythology of Alfred the vehicle of its opposition politics.
literary_significance: It is the most successful of the century's literary masques and the source of the song that became the anthem of the naval nation, and it shows the Augustan language of liberty converted into entertainment.
attribution_notes: Uncontested as Thomson's, the music being another hand's; the closing ode has been separately credited to the poet.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1740 with the accompanying ode; the private performance at the prince's seat is placed in the years immediately preceding the print, and its exact date is disputed and so left null here.

title: Sophonisba
description: Thomson's regular tragedy of the Carthaginian princess who chooses death rather than the Roman triumph, written deliberately in the observance of the unities and in the manner of the antique and French classical drama.
plot_or_argument: Sophonisba, taken between the rival African princes and the advancing Rome, is given by the conqueror to the suitor she must not love; she disappoints both by choosing the poison, and the play closes on the spectacle of her constant death.
narrative_structure: Five acts of strict regularity, with the set dying scene as the prepared catastrophe and the political argument of the rival parties supplying the tension.
principal_characters: Sophonisba; Syphax; Masinissa; Scipio; the attendants of the captive princess
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of studied smoothness, with the formal expiring dialogue of the last scene.
historical_context: Acted at Drury Lane in the season of Thomson's struggle with the theatres and of the debate over classical regularity, when the Racine model and the unities were being reasserted against the opera and the burletta.
literary_significance: It is the century's most complete English attempt at the classical regular tragedy, and its death scene became a byword for the calculated pathos of the closet and the stage.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1730 with the preface on the unities and the character of the ancient drama, which was separately reprinted as a critical piece; the performance history at Drury Lane is briefly recorded in that preface.

title: The Castle of Indolence
alternative_titles: The Castle of Indolence: An Allegorical Poem
description: Thomson's last and most finished allegorical poem, in the Spenserian measure: a knight is allured into the castle of Indolence, its slumber, its luxury and its self-consuming sweetness, and is delivered by the sight of the wizard's own punishment and of the castle's fall.
plot_or_argument: Two companions, the lover of labour and the lover of ease, come to the enchanted castle; the slumbry of its inhabitants, the pleasures of its gardens and the tales of its enchanter's love hold the indolent guest fast, until the philosophy of the active life and the destruction of the place recover him to virtue.
narrative_structure: Two cantos of continuous allegorical narrative, with the inserted tale of the enchanter and his fair one, the personified crew of the castle and the moral conclusion.
principal_characters: the two guests of the castle; the enchanter of the place and his fair one; the personified indolence and her crew
meter_and_prosody: The nine-line Spenserian stanza, revived by Thomson for this poem and used with a sensuous richness of sound that made the measure a permanent option for English allegory.
historical_context: Conceived in the early 1730s as a burlesque of the poet's own company and long retouched before its publication in the year of his death, when the Spenserian revival, the poetry of retirement and the moral argument about industry were all active.
literary_significance: It restored the Spenserian stanza to English verse, and it remains the period's most complete poem on the temptation of ease, answering the season's own moral economy with an allegory of the unspent life.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Published in May 1748 with the accompanying short poems; the several drafts and the project's long history are traced in the modern editions from the manuscript evidence.

title: The Revenge
description: Young's first tragedy, a blank-verse drama of jealous error in a Spanish and Moorish setting, in which a husband's belief in his wife's guilt destroys the innocent and himself; the play that introduced the century's high pathos of conjugal jealousy.
plot_or_argument: A Moorish and court intrigue, an intercepted letter and a treacherous third party work upon a husband's jealousy until the accused wife's constancy is proved only by her death, and revenge falls instead upon the author of the slander.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intrigue with the surprise of the false evidence and the discovery scene, closing on the death of the innocent and the ruin of the jealous.
principal_characters: the jealous husband; the accused and faithful wife; the artificer of the slander; the Moors and courtiers about them
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of passionate declamation, with the broken apostrophe, the long simile and the sententious close.
historical_context: Brought out on the London stage at the opening of the decade, in the season when the reformed regular tragedy of Rowe and the new musical entertainment competed for the same house; Young had attached himself to the great families of the governing interest, and the play's success began his long dependence on patronage.
literary_significance: It is the earliest considerable English tragedy of suspicion and of injured female constancy, and it carried the pathetic drama of The Fair Penitent into the domestic and conjugal register the century preferred.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1721; Young afterwards reworked the play for a later provincial revival, and the texts of the two states differ in length and in the handling of the catastrophe.

title: The Brothers
description: Young's domestic tragedy of two brothers, one of whom is condemned for a capital offence against a family's honour, drawn from the recent criminal case reported in the ordinary accounts of the town.
plot_or_argument: A seduced woman's accusation, a mistaken identity and the pursuit of the brothers through the stages of flight, trial and sentence bring one to the scaffold, while the father's anguish and the brother's devotion fill the play's intervals of pathos.
narrative_structure: Five acts of domestic calamity in the plainest tragic manner, with the trial and the execution as the two public crises framing the family's private distress.
principal_characters: the two brothers; the injured woman; the father; the judges and officers of the law
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse deliberately reduced to the nearest speech of grief, with the short exclamatory line and the address to the sufferer.
historical_context: Written and acted in the year of the Beggar's Opera's triumph, when the criminal case on the stage and in the ordinary was a popular species and when the controversy over laughing and sentimental comedy was opening.
literary_significance: It is the founding example of the English tragedy of the gallows and of the middle-rank family, the dramatic complement to Lillo's London merchant, and it fixed Young's reputation as the poet of mourning.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1728 with the dedication to a great name of the administration; the contemporary criminal case that suggested the plot is identified in the modern accounts of the play rather than in the printed text.

title: The Complaint, or, Night Thoughts on Life, Death and Immortality
alternative_titles: The Complaint: or, Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality
description: Young's long meditative poem on the night, death and the immortal life, spoken by a grieving soul under the patronage of the personified Night: the central work of the century's cultivation of melancholy and of the thought of death.
plot_or_argument: Across nine nights the poet addresses Night, the stars, the tomb and his own losses, passes through the tales of the ruined house, the physician and the fallen ambition, and rises from the meditation on mortality to the argument for immortality, the proof of religion and the triumph over the fear of death.
narrative_structure: A serial of nine numbered nights, each a continuous meditation with the inset narrative and the address to an auditor, first issued one by one and afterwards collected.
principal_characters: the poet; the personified Night and her daughters; the auditor of the tales; the dead whom the poem mourns
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines of great variety, with the abrupt short line, the capitalised abstraction, the exclamation and the suspended period of the night piece.
historical_context: Issued in the season of the century's mourning culture, the burial-ground and the fashionable garden, and in the same years as the debate over enthusiasm, ridicule and the reality of religion; the separate numbers were sold as they appeared and were gathered into a single poem as it grew.
literary_significance: It made the gloomy meditative night-piece the most influential English verse form of the later eighteenth century, supplied the imagery of the graveyard and the ruin to the Gothic, and was read across Europe in translation.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The first night was printed in 1742 and the series was completed in the middle of the decade, with the collected issue and a later revised state of the author's own; Blake's illustrated edition belongs to the closing years of the century.

title: Conjectures on Original Composition
alternative_titles: Conjectures on Original Composition in a Letter to a Friend
description: Young's critical essay on original genius, arguing that the great writer is made by nature and by his own industry rather than by the rules and the imitation of the ancients, and that an original composition is the only true growth of a literary nation.
plot_or_argument: The letter distinguishes the original from the imitation writer, compares the modern scholar to the child of a later age who is dwarfed by his parents, pleads the cause of native genius and of the invention that copies nature rather than books, and closes on the religious dignity of the creative mind.
narrative_structure: A continuous epistolary argument in numbered reflections, with the aphoristic proposition and the analogy carrying the sequence.
literary_form: critical essay in the form of a letter
meter_and_prosody: Aphoristic prose of the maxims and the numbered head, with the sustained metaphor of growth, nature and the child.
historical_context: Published in the same years as the first fragments of the Gaelic forgeries and of the debate on barbarism and genius, when the rules of taste were being displaced by the theory of original composition; Young's essay gave that theory its most quotable English statement.
literary_significance: It is the charter of the cult of genius in English criticism, translated into German almost at once and used by the romantic theorists and by the continent's argument about originality.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1759 in a pamphlet of a few score pages and reprinted with the author's later poems; the enlarged issue with the additions belongs to the closing years of the century.

title: A Paraphrase upon Part of the Book of Job
alternative_titles: A Paraphrase on Part of the Book of Job
A Paraphrase upon the Book of Job
description: Young's late blank-verse paraphrase of Job, which turns the patriarch's trial into a further Night Thought on affliction, the silence of providence and the immortality of the sufferer.
plot_or_argument: The paraphrase follows the argument of Job and his friends, the adversary's license and the calamities of the righteous man, and reads the poem as a proof of patience and of a life to come, ending in the restoration and the moral application.
narrative_structure: A continuous poetic paraphrase of the biblical book, with the speeches of Job, the friends and the divine answer rendered in the manner of the Complaint.
principal_characters: Job; the friends of Job; the adversary; the voice out of the whirlwind
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic and Youngian manner, with the inflated period and the apostrophic interruption.
historical_context: Published in the closing years of Young's life, in the season of the argument from the suffering of the righteous, of the Job revivals in devotional poetry and of his own quarrel with the critics of the Complaint.
literary_significance: It is the last great English verse paraphrase of Job before the century's end, and it completes the meditation on affliction and immortality which the Complaint had opened.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the pamphlet was issued anonymously and the author's name is supplied by the known signature of his other pieces.
bibliographical_notes: The date of the first impression is given here from the standard accounts and is approximate; the piece was subsequently reprinted with the collected poems.

title: Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College
description: Gray's ode written at Cambridge and looking over the playing fields of his old school, where the sports of the boys become the image of a life of unremembered cares and of the manhood that awaits them.
plot_or_argument: The poet watches the boys at their games from the far side of the river, asks them to be happy while they are ignorant of their years, reviews the passions and the miseries of after life, and ends by committing the ignorant and the unhappy to Forgetfulness.
narrative_structure: A stanced reflective ode progressing from the prospect and the apostrophe to the generalisation of human misery and the closing address to Forgetfulness.
principal_characters: the boys of Eton at their games; the personified passions and powers of the closing stanzas; the poet as spectator
meter_and_prosody: Quatrains of iambic five-beat lines with the alternate rhyme, the stanza form Gray carried to perfection in the Elegy; the diction is plain and the cadence restrained.
historical_context: Written in the year of the Elegy's beginnings and of Gray's residence at Cambridge, in the season when the schoolboy poem, the meditation on childhood and the reflection on future ill were becoming the topics of the descriptive lyric.
literary_significance: It gave English poetry its durable image of childhood seen from without, and its stanza and its turn of reflection are the direct preparation for the Elegy Written in a Country Church-Yard.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Composition is dated by Gray's own account of the year of writing; the first printing belongs to the collected issue of his poems in the middle of the century's fourth decade, and the copy-text of that issue differs slightly from the later editions.

title: Elegy Written in a Country Church-Yard
alternative_titles: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
description: Gray's meditation on the humble dead of a village churchyard, which reads the close of the day and the unremembered rustics as the proof that poverty hides merit, that the great die unknown to the poor, and that the tomb keeps its deposit without distinction.
plot_or_argument: The curfew and the closing light leave the thoughtful man among the mounds; he pictures the lives the villagers were denied, the unbeached and unpraised worth and beauty that lie there, and prays that the neglected poor may find in his own low verse a memorial; the meditation turns at last upon a fellow mourner cut short of his years, and the poem closes with an epitaph.
narrative_structure: A continuous stanced meditation from the landscape of the evening through the general reflection to the wish for the poet's own memorial and the closing epitaph
principal_characters: the dead of the churchyard; the rustic forefathers and the unnoticed women of the village; the neglected talent and the mute monument; the youth of the epitaph
meter_and_prosody: Quatrains of iambic five-beat lines in the Latin elegiac manner of the century's translation of the classics, with the balanced close, the postponed adjective and the hush of the evening stanza.
historical_context: Printed in the middle years of the century's quarrel over the gloomy and the descriptive lyric, in the circle of the graveyard taste and of the antiquarian interest in the churchyard monument, and after the publication of the Eton ode had made the meditative stanza Gray's own.
literary_significance: It is the most quoted and most imitated English poem of the century, the central document of the culture of feeling and of the thought of the obscure dead, and the schoolroom text by which several generations learned the elegiac temper.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed as a quarto and in a monthly magazine in 1751, with the companion pieces; the traditional account of its origin at the village of the poet's mother places the earliest lines in the fourth decade, and the several states of the text differ in a few lines.

title: The Progress of Poesy
description: Gray's Pindaric ode on the migration of poetry through the Greek colonies and their states, and its at last arrival in Britain, written in the measures he studied in the old French and Italian imitations of Pindar.
plot_or_argument: Poetry, restrained long in Egypt and in the East, bursts out among the colonies of Ionia and Doria, keeps court with the legislator and the victor, and passes through the ages of Greek and Roman decay at the coming of the northern power, till the Muse is received in Britain under the patronage of the ruling house.
narrative_structure: A paired strophe, antistrophe and epode structure in three parts, with the strophe of the ode carrying the historical advance and the epode the reflection.
principal_characters: Poesy and the Muse; the legislators and poets of the Greek states; the northern conqueror of the last stanzas
meter_and_prosody: The complex Grayian Pindaric stanza of unequal lines with a recurring scheme, modelled on the measures of the ancient ode as the eighteenth century reconstructed them.
historical_context: Written in the same year as The Bard and after a decade of Gray's study of the Pindaric measures, of the old English and of the Norse poetry, at the moment when the historical account of the progress of the arts was being written by the antiquarian critics.
literary_significance: It is the most accomplished English attempt to revive the Pindaric stanza as an instrument of cultural history, and it stands with The Bard as the monument of Gray's later ode.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1757 with The Bard in a small volume, to which the account of the measures was prefixed; an earlier ode on the same argument had circulated in manuscript in the fourth decade.

title: The Bard
description: Gray's Pindaric ode on the British bard and on the curse of the poet's people against an unworthy king, drawing upon the legends of the Welsh bards and on the imagery of the northern poetry.
plot_or_argument: The Muse of Poetry, driven from the courts of the degenerate, warns the people of the island and their bard; the royal house and its favourite are given over to ruin, and the bard's curse and the vanishing of his nation before the conqueror fill the closing strophes.
narrative_structure: Three parts of paired Pindaric stanzas, moving from the invocation and the warning to the curse and the prophetic conclusion.
principal_characters: the British bard; the Muse of Poetry; the unhappy king and his favourites; the people of the island
meter_and_prosody: The Grayian Pindaric measure, with the short opening line, the long swelling strophe and the emphatic epodic close; the stanzaic schemes are imitated from the Norse and Greek models he had studied.
historical_context: Written in the years of the antiquarian recovery of the Welsh and northern poetry, of the argument about the barbarous and the polished, and of the fashion for the curse of the poet, when the bard was becoming the figure of national and primitive genius.
literary_significance: It created the image of the bard as the prophet and arraigner of a nation, and together with the fragments and forgeries of the same decade it formed the mythology of primitive poetry for the romantic period.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed with The Progress of Poesy in 1757; the sources of the curse and of the legend are discussed in the note to the ode.

title: Hymn to Adversity
alternative_titles: Hymn to Adversity: Written on the Approach of Winter
description: Gray's short hymn addressed to Adversity as the grim daughter of Power and Wisdom, which thanks the harsh teacher for the discipline of sorrow and for the humanising effect of misfortune.
plot_or_argument: The hymn invokes Adversity, attends her from the throne of the supreme, and shows how her stern schooling teaches compassion, self-knowledge and the value of the fleeting good, closing with the prayer that her discipline may not be in vain.
narrative_structure: A regular stanced hymn of invocation, argument and prayer, following the order of the Horatian and the church hymn.
principal_characters: Adversity addressed as a power; the parent powers of Wisdom and of the chastening will
meter_and_prosody: Regular short stanzas of the hymn measure in the manner of the Horatian ode, with the clear close and the balanced personification.
historical_context: Written in the same year as the Eton ode, in the circle of the poet's college retirement and of the Horatian revival, and long read as a companion to the century's discipline of sorrow.
literary_significance: It is the most perfect English short hymn of the school of feeling, converting the stoic and Christian argument of affliction into a regular lyric.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Composition is dated by the poet's own inscription of the year; the first printing could not be verified for this record and the publication date is left null, though the hymn certainly belongs to the collected issues of Gray's verse between 1748 and 1768.

title: The Fatal Sisters
alternative_titles: The Fatal Sisters: A Translation from the Norse
description: Gray's imitated translation of an old Norse poem of the women of the battle, in which the fatal sisters sing the names of the doomed and the course of the fight while they ply the wound and the hair.
plot_or_argument: The daughters of the whirlwind and the battle chant their terrible weaving of the fates of the warriors, name the king whose hour is come and the land that is to be won, and ride away to the north and to the night after the song.
narrative_structure: A short series of antiphonal stanzas of the imitated Norse measure, with the refrain and the enumeration of the slain.
principal_characters: the fatal sisters of the battle; the king whose doom is chanted; the warriors of the two hosts
meter_and_prosody: The short paired lines of the reconstructed northern measure, with the heavy alliteration and the repeated burden.
historical_context: Written in the same year as The Bard out of Gray's study of the Danish and Norse poetry in the antiquarian editions, at the moment when the northern and the primitive were being made the models of a new sublimity.
literary_significance: It introduced the imagery and the machinery of the northern mythology into English verse, and it is the most exact of the century's poetic reconstructions of primitive poetry.
attribution_notes: Uncontested as Gray's, though the piece is an imitation rather than a literal translation and the identification of his Norse original is a matter of the antiquarian scholarship of the following century.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1757; the wording of the title page's claim of translation is given here from the short title familiar in the editions, and the exact wording of the first issue has not been collated.

title: The Descent of Odin
alternative_titles: The Descent of Odin: A Translation from the Norse
description: Gray's imitated translation of the northern poem in which Odin raises a dead prophetess from her grave to learn the fate that awaits him, a short dramatic lyric of the nether world.
plot_or_argument: The father of the northern gods descends to the boundaries of the dead and compels the sealed prophetess to speak; her answers tell of a grief among the powers of light and of the doom that is coming upon them, and the vision closes with the dread of the hour.
narrative_structure: A brief dialogue of the questioner and the raised dead, in the staves of the imitated measure.
principal_characters: Odin; the prophetess raised from the dead; the powers and the doomed of the northern mythology
meter_and_prosody: The short lines and the alternate rhyme of the reconstructed Norse measure, with the abrupt address and the reiterate question.
historical_context: Written with The Fatal Sisters from Gray's antiquarian reading of the Edda in the editions then new to English students, in the decade which made the northern mythology a resource of poetry.
literary_significance: It is the earliest English poem to make the mythology of the Edda a poetic machinery, and it prepared the northern sublime of the following century.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, with the same qualification as The Fatal Sisters: the piece is an imitated translation, and the identification of the source poem rests on later scholarship.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in 1757 with the accompanying odes; the exact wording of the title page's claim of translation has not been collated for this record.

title: Ode on the Spring
description: Gray's reflective ode on the returning year, in which the music and the gladness of the spring become an occasion for the examination of the poet's own cold and disordered mind.
plot_or_argument: The bird, the breeze and the opening year awake the senses and the fancy of every creature but the poet, who finds himself incapable of the spring's gladness, and turns the season to the argument that Wisdom's precepts leave the heart untaught while the social affections are allowed their play.
narrative_structure: A stanced description passing into self-examination and a closing moral address, in the order of the descriptive ode.
principal_characters: the creatures of the spring in their gladness; the poet as the exception; the personified powers of the moral argument
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic lyric ode in the smooth measures of the descriptive school, with the short line of the bird passage and the longer period of the reflection.
historical_context: Printed with the Eton ode in the first collected issue of Gray's poems, in the years when the description of the seasons and the philosophy of the affections were joining in the lyric.
literary_significance: It is Gray's earliest complete statement of the argument that feeling, not rule, is the life of virtue, and it stands between Thomson's seasons and the meditative lyrics of the following decade.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The date of composition is assigned from the poet's own account of the year and is approximate; the first printing belongs to the collected poems of the fourth decade.

title: Persian Eclogues
description: Collins's earliest published verses: two short eclogues after the Persian, in which the oriental scene of the garden, the cup and the beloved carries the lover's complaint and the picture of the poet's own retirement.
plot_or_argument: The eclogues set a lover's lament and the description of the Eastern season against the soft music of the pipe and the garden, with the poet's own wish for a like solitude and an unnoticed death.
narrative_structure: Two independent short eclogues in the dialogue and complaint manner, joined only by their oriental scene.
principal_characters: the lover of the complaint; the beloved and the attendants of the oriental scene; the poet in his retirement
literary_form: eclogue pair after the eastern manner
meter_and_prosody: Short lyric stanzas and couplets of the oriental imitation, with the soft recurring line of the song passages.
historical_context: Published in a monthly magazine in the year of the vogue for the eastern tale and the Persian letters, when the imitation of eastern models was one of the recognised schools of English lyric.
literary_significance: They show the formation of Collins's lyric manner out of the oriental fashion, and they prepared the softer and more melancholy measures of the odes of the following decade.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The poet's Eastern obligations are stated in the pieces themselves; the identification of the precise Persian originals is not asserted here, and the first printing is that of a magazine of 1742.

title: Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegorical Subjects
alternative_titles: Odes, on Several Descriptive and Allegorical Subjects
description: Collins's collected odes, the volume that gathered the descriptive and allegorical pieces of the previous years and made him the lyric poet of the century's transition from the couplet to the imaginative ode.
plot_or_argument: The volume passes through the allegorical personages of Fear, Simplicity and the Passions, the descriptive prospects and the ode for music, and the poet's own meditations on retirement and on the fate of the imaginative mind.
narrative_structure: A collected sequence of independent odes, arranged with a preface and the short essay on the nature of the ode, without continuous narrative.
principal_characters: the personified Passions of the ode for music; Fear and the allegorical attendants; the poet as the meditant speaker
meter_and_prosody: A range of measures from the smooth couplet and the lyrical stanza to the complex ode of the Pindaric and the blank-verse march, with the deliberate variety of the volume's arrangement.
historical_context: Issued at the close of the decade of the odes, in the season of Akenside's and Gray's rival experiments, of the quarrel over the Pindaric measure and of the new taste for the descriptive and allegorical lyric.
literary_significance: It established the short English ode as a form of imaginative suggestion rather than of argument, and its influence on the lyrical revival of the following century was continuous.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The title page reads Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegorical Subjects, printed for the London bookseller whose name stands upon it; the sheets were put about at the end of 1746 and copies carry the date 1747, and the earlier issue under a shorter title has also been reported.

title: Ode on the Poetical Character
description: Collins's ode on what the true poet is and how his imagination is made, arguing that the poetic character depends on a gift of fancy and on the union of learning, passion and sensibility.
plot_or_argument: The ode asks by what power the poet raises his scene above the world, reviews the ancient makers as the company of the chosen, and concludes that the imaginative faculty and the ear of the poet are the conditions of his office.
narrative_structure: A continuous stanced argument with the invocation, the review of the ancient poets and the closing definition.
principal_characters: the poet of the character; Fancy and the imaginative powers; the ancient bards of the review
meter_and_prosody: Varied lyric stanzas in the Collinsian manner, with the long winding line of the imaginative passage and the sententious close.
historical_context: Written in the years of the argument over genius, imitation and the faculty of the poet, when the theory of fancy and imagination was being formed out of the Addisonian account of the pleasures of the imagination.
literary_significance: It is one of the century's shortest and most concentrated definitions of the imaginative poet, and its account of fancy was a source for the later theory of the secondary imagination.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the collected odes of 1746; it had been circulated in manuscript and the versions differ in the order and the number of the stanzas.

title: The Passions: An Ode for Music
description: Collins's ode for music, in which the several passions answer the calls of the instruments and the chief among them is given the mastery of the hearer's soul.
plot_or_argument: The passions are summoned in turn by the music, each answering in its own measure, from the plainest to the most heroic and the most melancholy, until the ruling passion closes the concert in the triumph of the mind it has possessed.
narrative_structure: An ode of invocation and succession, the stanzas distributed among the several passions in the manner of the musical entertainment.
principal_characters: the personified Passions; Music as the summoning power; the ruling passion of the close
meter_and_prosody: A series of contrasting lyric measures, each stanza adapted to the passion and to the air it imitates, in the tradition of the Dryden and Handel ode.
historical_context: Written in the decade when the English ode for music was being revived for the London concerts and for the Handel oratorio, and when the theory of the passions supplied the programme of such pieces.
literary_significance: It is the most accomplished of the century's odes on the powers of music and the passions, and it carries the musical ode from the Dryden manner to the lyric variety of the following generation.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the collected odes of 1746, in the state of the text established there; the piece was long known from the volume and its earlier manuscript history is not asserted here.

title: The Pleasures of Imagination
alternative_titles: The Pleasures of Imagination, a Poem
description: Akenside's didactic poem on the imagination, developing Addison's account of the pleasures of the mind into a philosophical and moral system in which the beauties of the senses, of the passions and of virtue are the discipline of an educated soul.
plot_or_argument: The poem traces the workings of the mind in the perception of greatness, novelty and beauty, passes to the pleasures of the passions and of the moral sense, and closes with the cultivation of taste as the preparation for virtue and for the happiness of a well-ordered mind.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in books, first issued in one book and afterwards enlarged, with the philosophical analysis, the illustrative description and the apostrophe interwoven.
principal_characters: the poet's Muse and the powers of imagination; the mind of the spectator; the personified Beauty and the moral sense
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed five-beat lines of the Thomson and Milton school, with the long descriptive period and the abstract noun in place of the concrete image.
historical_context: Written in the years of the association of ideas, of Hutcheson's moral sense and of the debate over the imagination begun by the Spectator essays, by Akenside's physician and patron circle and by the new metaphysical writing of the Scottish professors.
literary_significance: It is the most ambitious attempt of the mid-century to fuse the theory of taste, the philosophy of mind and the poem of religion, and its blank verse and its vocabulary of the imagination passed to the romantic theorists.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The first book was printed in 1744; the complete three-book poem was put out only after the author's death from a long-revised text, and the several states of the earlier book differ.

title: Odes on Several Subjects
description: Akenside's volume of odes, raising the Pindaric and the lyrical experiment of the decade into a book: the hymns, the lyrical addresses and the imitations of the ancient measures with the short essay on the odical composition.
plot_or_argument: The odes pass from the hymn and the address to the powers of knowledge and of the mind, through the lyrical and the descriptive pieces, to the Pindaric attempt at the sublime and the moral reflection.
narrative_structure: A collected sequence of independent odes with a prefatory account of the measures, without continuous narrative.
principal_characters: the personified powers and virtues of the hymns; the poet as the worshipper and the moralist
meter_and_prosody: A deliberate variety of measures, including the strophe and antistrophe of the Pindaric experiment and the shorter hymn stanza, with the long line of the sublime passage.
historical_context: Published in the year of Collins's odes and just before Gray's Pindarics, in the decade's experiment with the ode, the hymn and the northern and ancient measures; the volume was attacked in the same years by the critics of the new Pindaricism.
literary_significance: It records the mid-century attempt to refound English lyric on the ancient and the enthusiastic measures, and it supplies the hymn and the sublime as the two poles of the odes of the period.
attribution_notes: Uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: The volume is generally assigned to the middle of the decade, with some accounts placing the earliest sheets a year earlier; the date is given here as approximate and the order of the pieces varies in the copies.

title: The Epistle to Curio
description: Akenside's political verse epistle, the fiercest party attack of the mid-century, denouncing the statesman who passed from the opposition to the administration and warning the nation against the corruption of its liberty.
plot_or_argument: The poet addresses Curio as the traitor to the public cause, traces his progress from the patriotic platform to the rewards of the court, and sets the example of the true patriot against the train of ministers, place-holders and corrupt senators.
narrative_structure: A single long epistle of invective, moving from the character of the minister to the history of his treason and to the general argument about the fate of British liberty.
principal_characters: Curio the converted minister; the poet as the patriot monitor; the court and the corrupted senate
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplet of the Juvenalian and Swiftian hardness, with the long arraigning period and the closing sententia.
historical_context: Written in the year of the fall of the long administration and published at the moment when the conversion of the old country leaders into the new ministry seemed to the patriot writers the ruin of the country cause; the pamphlet presented itself as an old manuscript now first printed.
literary_significance: It is the ablest of the century's verse political attacks and the work by which Akenside's public career as a moral and political poet began, and the person intended was understood at once by the party readers of the year.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously and long uncertain in its authorship, with other names proposed by its enemies; Akenside's claim is established by his circle and by the manuscript evidence, though he is said to have wished the piece suppressed in later life.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in 1744 with the pretence of an earlier composition date upon the title; the identification of Curio with a leading minister of the age is the settled modern reading and is not drawn from the printed text.
